stimulus: Harlow Field's airport authority enforces a simple scheduling policy: whenever a flight departs after midnight, it is a cargo flight. The authority's published timetable includes Flight 88, a service that carries passengers only and no freight. The timetable also lists several cargo flights that depart in the late afternoon.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Every cargo flight on the timetable departs after midnight.
choices.B: Flight 88 does not depart after midnight.
choices.C: Flight 88 departs in the late afternoon.
choices.D: Some passenger-only flights on the timetable depart after midnight.
choices.E: Every flight that does not depart after midnight carries passengers only.

explanations.A: Reversal. The policy makes after-midnight departure sufficient for being a cargo flight, not the other way around; the late-afternoon cargo flights show cargo flights need not leave after midnight.
explanations.B: Correct. After midnight leads to cargo. Flight 88 is not a cargo flight, so by the contrapositive it cannot depart after midnight.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Flight 88 is shown not to leave after midnight, but nothing places it in the late afternoon rather than, say, the morning.
explanations.D: Opposite. A passenger-only flight is not a cargo flight, so it cannot depart after midnight under the policy.
explanations.E: Denying the sufficient condition. Not departing after midnight triggers no rule, and the late-afternoon cargo flights directly contradict this choice.

keyTakeaway: Not the necessary condition means not the sufficient condition; the contrapositive is the one backward move that is safe.
predictionHint: Flight 88 is not cargo, so it cannot be after midnight.

stimulus: At Greenway Nursery, any seedling that has been hardened off survives transplanting. Last week a grower transplanted all of the seedlings in Tray 4 into the open beds. By the end of the week, several of those seedlings had died.
stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.A: Every Tray 4 seedling that survived the transplant had been hardened off.
choices.B: Most of the seedlings in Tray 4 had not been hardened off.
choices.C: At least one seedling in Tray 4 had not been hardened off.
choices.D: Seedlings that are not hardened off never survive transplanting.
choices.E: The Tray 4 seedlings died because they were transplanted too early.

explanations.A: Reversal. Being hardened off is sufficient for survival; it is not stated to be necessary, so survivors could include seedlings that were not hardened off.
explanations.B: Extreme. One death proves at least one unhardened seedling, but 'several' deaths out of an unknown number do not show most were unhardened.
explanations.C: Correct. Hardened off leads to survival, so a seedling that died was not hardened off (contrapositive). Several died, so at least one was not.
explanations.D: Denying the sufficient condition. The rule says nothing about what happens to seedlings that were not hardened off.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Timing is never mentioned, and the passage gives no cause for the deaths.

keyTakeaway: A failure on the right side of an arrow proves a failure on the left side, and nothing more.
predictionHint: The ones that died were not hardened off.

stimulus: Registrar: Dara applied to the Calloway honors cohort in the autumn and was interviewed by two faculty members. Every student admitted to the cohort has completed the two-term writing sequence. It follows that Dara was not admitted to the cohort.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Dara has not completed the two-term writing sequence.
choices.B: Dara's interviewers were not impressed by her application.
choices.C: Every student who has completed the two-term writing sequence is admitted to the cohort.
choices.D: Every student who was not admitted to the cohort has not completed the two-term writing sequence.
choices.E: Dara will complete the two-term writing sequence before the next admissions cycle.

explanations.A: Correct. Admitted leads to completed the sequence. If Dara has not completed it, the contrapositive gives not admitted.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The interviewers' impressions are not connected by any stated rule to admission.
explanations.C: Reversal. It makes completion sufficient for admission, but the stated rule makes completion necessary; this does not touch Dara.
explanations.D: Denying the sufficient condition (the inverse of the rule). It speaks of students who were not admitted, which presupposes the conclusion rather than supporting it.
explanations.E: Out of scope. A future completion says nothing about whether she has completed the sequence now, and would actually be compatible with admission.

keyTakeaway: To conclude 'not X' from 'X requires Y', the missing premise is 'not Y'.
predictionHint: Admission requires the sequence, so Dara must lack the sequence.

stimulus: The Pellam Orchestra gives six concerts each season. Every concert the orchestra gives in Rowan Hall is a benefit concert. A benefit concert is held only if a corporate sponsor has been secured for it. The orchestra's March concert had no corporate sponsor.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: The March concert was a benefit concert held outside Rowan Hall.
choices.B: Any concert the orchestra gives outside Rowan Hall has a corporate sponsor.
choices.C: Every benefit concert the orchestra gives is held in Rowan Hall.
choices.D: The March concert was held somewhere other than Rowan Hall because no sponsor could be found.
choices.E: The March concert was not held in Rowan Hall.

explanations.A: Opposite. The chain Rowan Hall, benefit, sponsor runs backward from the missing sponsor to 'not a benefit concert', so the March concert was not a benefit concert at all.
explanations.B: Denying the sufficient condition. The rules say what Rowan Hall concerts require; they say nothing about concerts held elsewhere.
explanations.C: Reversal. Rowan Hall leads to benefit, not benefit to Rowan Hall; benefit concerts could be given elsewhere.
explanations.D: Half right. The venue claim follows, but the stated reason does not; the passage never says why the concert was placed where it was.
explanations.E: Correct. No sponsor means not a benefit concert (contrapositive of the second rule), and not a benefit concert means not in Rowan Hall (contrapositive of the first).

keyTakeaway: Chain the arrows, then run the contrapositive of the whole chain from the denied end.
predictionHint: No sponsor, so not benefit, so not in Rowan Hall.

stimulus: Under the Oresund Accord, a member state may invoke the emergency provision only if it has filed a notice of hardship. Moreover, no member state that has filed a notice of hardship also seeks a tariff waiver. Hence Brannoch, a member state, cannot invoke the emergency provision.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Brannoch has filed a notice of hardship.
choices.B: Brannoch does not seek a tariff waiver.
choices.C: Every member state that does not seek a tariff waiver has filed a notice of hardship.
choices.D: Brannoch itself seeks a tariff waiver.
choices.E: Brannoch is not one of the original member states of the Accord.

explanations.A: Opposite. Filing a notice is necessary for invoking the provision, so this would leave open that Brannoch can invoke it rather than rule it out.
explanations.B: Affirming the necessary condition. Not seeking a waiver is what a filer of notice must do, so it is compatible with Brannoch having filed; it does not show that no notice was filed.
explanations.C: Reversal. It runs the second rule backward and says nothing about Brannoch itself.
explanations.D: Correct. Filed notice leads to no waiver, so seeking a waiver means no notice was filed (contrapositive). No notice means the provision cannot be invoked (contrapositive of the first rule).
explanations.E: Out of scope. Nothing in either rule depends on a state's original or later membership.

keyTakeaway: When the conclusion needs 'no notice', look for the premise that is the contrapositive of a rule, not the one that merely sounds consistent with it.
predictionHint: Brannoch must lack a notice; the second rule says waiver-seekers lack one.

stimulus: At the Veldt Observatory, any instrument that was calibrated this year is housed in the east dome, and any instrument used for the infrared survey is housed in the east dome as well. No instrument housed in the east dome is rated for field transport. The observatory's spectrograph is not housed in the east dome.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: The spectrograph was calibrated this year but is not used for the infrared survey.
choices.B: The spectrograph was not calibrated this year and is not used for the infrared survey.
choices.C: Every instrument housed in the east dome was either calibrated this year or used for the infrared survey.
choices.D: The spectrograph is rated for field transport.
choices.E: The spectrograph is the only instrument at the observatory that is not housed in the east dome.

explanations.A: Opposite. A calibrated instrument must be in the east dome, so a spectrograph outside it cannot have been calibrated this year.
explanations.B: Correct. Each of the two sufficient conditions leads to the east dome; being outside the east dome therefore rules out both, by the contrapositive of each rule.
explanations.C: Reversal. Both rules make the east dome necessary, not sufficient; instruments there may have been placed for other reasons.
explanations.D: Denying the sufficient condition. Only east dome instruments are said to lack field-transport ratings; being outside the dome triggers no rule.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Nothing indicates how many other instruments are housed outside the east dome.

keyTakeaway: When two arrows share a necessary condition, denying it denies both sufficient conditions; it never lets you go the other way.
predictionHint: Outside the east dome means neither calibrated nor infrared.

stimulus: Whenever mediation of a dispute fails, the dispute is referred to arbitration, and a dispute is referred to arbitration only if both parties to it have signed the submission agreement. In the Hollis-Mercer dispute, Mercer never signed the submission agreement.
stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.A: The Hollis-Mercer dispute was resolved through mediation.
choices.B: Hollis signed the submission agreement as well.
choices.C: Mediation of the Hollis-Mercer dispute failed, and the dispute then went unresolved.
choices.D: Any dispute whose parties have both signed the submission agreement is referred to arbitration.
choices.E: Mediation of the Hollis-Mercer dispute did not fail.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Did not fail' is all the chain gives; nothing says mediation took place or succeeded, so 'was resolved through mediation' goes beyond it.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Mercer's missing signature settles the matter regardless of whether Hollis signed.
explanations.C: Opposite. Failure would lead to arbitration, which would require Mercer's signature, so failure is ruled out.
explanations.D: Reversal. Both signatures are necessary for referral, not sufficient for it.
explanations.E: Correct. Failure leads to referral, and referral requires both signatures. Mercer did not sign, so no referral, so mediation did not fail.

keyTakeaway: Read a chain from the denied end back to the start: each step backward is a contrapositive.
predictionHint: No signature, so no referral, so mediation did not fail.

stimulus: Auditing firm memo: Each division submits a report every quarter. Every report that the auditors flag is returned to its author for revision. The Hargrove report contains a material misstatement. Therefore, the Hargrove report was returned to its author for revision.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Any report that the auditors do not flag is free of material misstatements.
choices.B: Any report that the auditors flag contains a material misstatement.
choices.C: Any report that is free of material misstatements goes unflagged by the auditors.
choices.D: Some reports returned to their authors for revision were not flagged by the auditors.
choices.E: Every report returned to its author for revision contains a material misstatement.

explanations.A: Correct. This is the contrapositive of 'misstatement leads to flagged'. With the first premise it gives misstatement, flagged, returned for revision.
explanations.B: Reversal. It says a flag implies a misstatement, which does not tell us that a report with a misstatement gets flagged.
explanations.C: Denying the sufficient condition. It says no misstatement leads to no flag, which is the inverse of what is needed and gives nothing about a report that has a misstatement.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant. Reports returned without a flag are consistent with the argument but do not connect the Hargrove misstatement to a flag.
explanations.E: Reversal. It runs the final link backward, from revision to misstatement, so a misstatement still never reaches revision.

keyTakeaway: The missing link in a conditional chain is the arrow from the given fact to the start of the stated rule, and it may be worded as a contrapositive.
predictionHint: Misstatement leads to flagged; look for that or its contrapositive.

stimulus: The Ferndale Museum's posted rules state that no visitor may enter the archive room without a staff escort. This afternoon the museum's guards report that every rule was obeyed by every visitor. Marisol, a visitor, spent part of the afternoon in the archive room.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Marisol is a member of the museum's staff.
choices.B: Every visitor who has a staff escort spent time in the archive room.
choices.C: Marisol entered the archive room with a staff escort.
choices.D: Marisol was not escorted by any staff member.
choices.E: Every visitor to the museum this afternoon had a staff escort.

explanations.A: Out of scope. The rule governs visitors, and Marisol is described as one.
explanations.B: Reversal. An escort is necessary for entering the archive room, not enough to ensure a visit there.
explanations.C: Correct. 'No entry without an escort' means entering leads to escort. Marisol entered and the rules were obeyed, so she had one.
explanations.D: Opposite. It contradicts the rule being obeyed.
explanations.E: Extreme. The rule concerns the archive room only; visitors elsewhere in the museum are unaffected.

keyTakeaway: 'No X without Y' means X requires Y; if X happened, Y happened.
predictionHint: Entered the archive room, so she had an escort.

stimulus: At the Aldergate cooperative, the only members who hold a vault key are members who have passed the security briefing. Only members who hold a vault key lead the weekend session. The cooperative has forty members, and its practices follow its bylaws without exception.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.A: Some member who has passed the security briefing does not hold a vault key.
choices.B: Some member who holds a vault key does not lead the weekend session.
choices.C: No member who has passed the security briefing leads the weekend session.
choices.D: Some member who leads the weekend session has not passed the security briefing.
choices.E: Some member who has not passed the security briefing does not hold a vault key.

explanations.A: Reversal trap, and it can be true. Passing the briefing is necessary for a key, not sufficient, so briefed members without keys are possible.
explanations.B: Reversal trap, and it can be true. Holding a key is required to lead, but nothing says every key holder leads.
explanations.C: Extreme, but it can be true. The rules do not require that anyone who passed the briefing leads, so it is possible that none of them does.
explanations.D: Correct. Leading requires a key, and a key requires passing the briefing. A leader who has not passed would violate the chain, so this cannot be true.
explanations.E: Can be true, and is in fact what the rule predicts for any member who has not passed. It is a statement the rules permit, so it is not the one that cannot be true.

keyTakeaway: 'The only X are Y' and 'only X do Z' both put the necessary condition after the word; the statement that cannot be true is the one that violates a necessary condition.
predictionHint: Lead, key, briefing: anyone leading without the briefing breaks the chain.

stimulus: Unless the forecast fails to call for clear skies, the Kestrel Orchestra holds its summer concert on the lawn rather than in the hall. Last July the orchestra held its summer concert in the hall, and its staff did so in accordance with its standing policy.
stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.A: The forecast for last July's concert failed to call for clear skies.
choices.B: The forecast for last July's concert called for rain.
choices.C: Whenever the forecast fails to call for clear skies, the orchestra holds its summer concert in the hall.
choices.D: The forecast for last July's concert called for clear skies, but the orchestra moved the concert indoors anyway.
choices.E: The orchestra holds its summer concert on the lawn only when the forecast calls for clear skies.

explanations.A: Correct. 'Unless the forecast fails to call for clear skies' means: if it does call for clear skies, the concert is on the lawn. The concert was in the hall, so the forecast did not call for clear skies.
explanations.B: Extreme. A forecast that fails to call for clear skies need not call for rain; it could say cloud or wind.
explanations.C: Denying the sufficient condition. The policy states what a clear-sky forecast produces, not what happens when the forecast is not clear.
explanations.D: Opposite. A clear-sky forecast leads to a lawn concert, and the staff followed policy, so the concert would not have been moved.
explanations.E: Reversal. The policy makes a clear forecast sufficient for the lawn, not necessary; the lawn could be used in other circumstances.

keyTakeaway: 'Unless' puts the negation of its clause on the sufficient side; if that clause is itself negative, the two negatives cancel.
predictionHint: Clear skies called for, so lawn. In the hall, so clear skies were not called for.

stimulus: Every candidate who wins the regional spelling contest has studied the official word list. Tomás has studied the official word list. Therefore, Tomás will win the regional spelling contest.
stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Anyone who completes the marathon course receives a finisher's medal. Priya completed the marathon course. Therefore, Priya received a finisher's medal.
choices.B: Every musician who earns a seat in the symphony practices daily. Lena practices daily. Therefore, Lena will earn a seat in the symphony.
choices.C: Every tenant who pays rent late is charged a fee. Wen did not pay rent late. Therefore, Wen was not charged a fee.
choices.D: Every hiker who reaches the summit carries a permit. Jonas does not carry a permit. Therefore, Jonas did not reach the summit.
choices.E: Three of the shops on Elm Street sold out of umbrellas on Monday. Therefore, most shops in the city sold out of umbrellas on Monday.

explanations.A: Opposite: this argument starts from the sufficient condition (completing the course) and concludes the necessary result (the medal). That is valid, so it cannot parallel a flawed argument.
explanations.B: Correct. The original runs Win -> Studied; Studied; therefore Win, treating a requirement as a guarantee. This choice runs Seat -> Practices; Practices; therefore Seat, with the same reversal and the same certain, predictive conclusion.
explanations.C: Half right: it is also a conditional error, but it denies the sufficient condition (Late -> Fee; not Late; so no Fee). The original affirms the necessary condition, a different direction of error.
explanations.D: Opposite: Summit -> Permit; no Permit; so no Summit is a valid contrapositive. A valid argument cannot share the original's flaw.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the flaw here is generalizing from a small sample, not a conditional error. It has no rule of the form 'every X has Y' at all.

keyTakeaway: In Parallel Flaw, diagram the original's error and its direction, then keep only the choice that makes the same move.
predictionHint: Winners all did X; this person did X; so this person will win. Match that reversal.

stimulus: Every applicant who submits the form by the deadline is considered for the fellowship. Raúl did not submit the form by the deadline. Therefore, Raúl is not considered for the fellowship.
stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Every shipment that contains lithium is inspected at the border. The crate from Oslo was inspected at the border. Therefore, the crate from Oslo contains lithium.
choices.B: Every pilot who flies the northern route carries extra fuel. Hana carries no extra fuel. Therefore, Hana does not fly the northern route.
choices.C: No intern is allowed in the laboratory without supervision. Dev is an intern. Therefore, Dev is not allowed in the laboratory without supervision.
choices.D: Any vehicle that exceeds the posted weight limit is turned away at the bridge. The truck ahead of us does not exceed the posted weight limit. Therefore, the truck will not be turned away at the bridge.
choices.E: Neighborhoods with more coffee shops have higher home prices. Therefore, opening more coffee shops raises the price of homes in a neighborhood.

explanations.A: Half right: also a conditional error, but it affirms the necessary result (inspected, so lithium). The original denies the sufficient condition, which is the opposite move.
explanations.B: Opposite: Northern -> Fuel; no Fuel; so no Northern is a valid contrapositive. Valid reasoning cannot parallel a flaw.
explanations.C: Opposite: a universal rule plus a member of the group, concluding the rule applies. That is valid.
explanations.D: Correct. The original runs Submit -> Considered; not Submit; so not Considered. This runs Exceeds -> Turned away; not Exceeds; so not Turned away. Both deny the sufficient condition and conclude the result will not occur.
explanations.E: Wrong part: this is a correlation-to-cause flaw with no conditional rule in it.

keyTakeaway: Denying the sufficient condition ('not A, so not B') and affirming the necessary one ('B, so A') are different errors; match the direction.
predictionHint: Rule A -> B, then 'not A, so not B.' Look for the same move.

stimulus: I asked the first twelve people who left the downtown fitness center on Saturday morning whether they enjoy vigorous exercise, and eleven said they do. Therefore, most residents of the city enjoy vigorous exercise.
stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: The first ten shoppers leaving the organic market on Sunday said they prefer locally grown produce. Therefore, most people in the region prefer locally grown produce.
choices.B: A polling firm phoned 1,500 households chosen at random from the county's records, and 62 percent said they support the transit bond. Therefore, a majority of county households probably support the bond.
choices.C: Towns in the valley with more public libraries have higher average test scores. Therefore, building libraries is what raises a town's test scores.
choices.D: Each of the five committee members is a skilled negotiator. Therefore, the committee as a whole will negotiate skillfully.
choices.E: Everyone who wins the raffle holds a ticket. Sana holds a ticket. Therefore, Sana will win the raffle.

explanations.A: Correct. Both argue about a whole population from people met at one place that favors the trait (an organic market, a fitness center). The sample is unrepresentative, and the conclusion is the same 'most' claim.
explanations.B: Opposite: households chosen at random from the county's records form a representative sample, so the inference is reasonable. A sound argument cannot share the original's flaw.
explanations.C: Wrong part: this confuses correlation with cause. It is not a sampling error.
explanations.D: Wrong part: this assumes that what is true of each part is true of the whole. It involves no sample.
explanations.E: Wrong part: this is a conditional error (affirming the necessary condition), not a sampling error.

keyTakeaway: A sample drawn from a place that selects for the trait cannot support a claim about the whole population.
predictionHint: Unrepresentative handful of people, stretched to 'most people overall.'

stimulus: Each of the engineers on the Delta Bridge project is the most experienced in her specialty in the state. Therefore, the Delta Bridge engineering team must be the most experienced engineering team in the state.
stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Two of the cheeses sampled from the dairy's latest batch were sharper than the label advertises. Therefore, the dairy's cheese is generally sharper than advertised.
choices.B: Every orchard that is certified organic avoids synthetic pesticides. Greenfield Orchard is not certified organic. Therefore, Greenfield Orchard uses synthetic pesticides.
choices.C: Households that own more books tend to have children with larger vocabularies. So owning more books gives children larger vocabularies.
choices.D: Every goalkeeper on the team is over six feet tall. Marek is a goalkeeper on the team. Therefore, Marek is over six feet tall.
choices.E: Each of the dancers in the Aldous Company is the finest in the region at her style. Therefore, the Aldous Company must be the finest dance company in the region.

explanations.A: Wrong part: this generalizes from two samples to the whole batch. It does not move from members to a group.
explanations.B: Half right: it is a flawed argument, but the flaw is denying the sufficient condition of a conditional. Nothing here concerns members versus a group.
explanations.C: Wrong part: this takes a correlation to show cause, a different flaw.
explanations.D: Opposite: a rule about every goalkeeper applied to one goalkeeper is valid.
explanations.E: Correct. Each member of the group has a superlative quality, and the argument concludes the group has it too. That is the same part-to-whole error, with the same 'must be' conclusion.

keyTakeaway: Being the best at each part does not make the whole the best; a group can be more than, or less than, the sum of its members.
predictionHint: Every member is the best, so the group is the best.

stimulus: A team advances to the national finals only if it wins its regional round. The Ridgemont Rockets won their regional round. Therefore, the Rockets will advance to the national finals.
stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: A student may enroll in the advanced seminar only if she has completed the prerequisite course. Keiko has not completed the prerequisite course. Therefore, Keiko may not enroll in the advanced seminar.
choices.B: A flight is cleared for departure only if its crew has been certified by the medical office. The crew of Flight 214 has been certified by the medical office. Therefore, Flight 214 will probably be cleared for departure.
choices.C: A restaurant is permitted to reopen only if it passes a health inspection. The Alder Street Café passed its health inspection. Therefore, the Alder Street Café will be permitted to reopen.
choices.D: A contractor is hired for the project only if she is licensed. Mei was not hired for the project. Therefore, Mei is not licensed.
choices.E: The two apartments I toured in the Fairview building both had broken heaters. Therefore, most apartments in the Fairview building have broken heaters.

explanations.A: Opposite: Enroll -> Prerequisite; no Prerequisite; so no Enroll is a valid contrapositive of an 'only if' rule.
explanations.B: Half right: it makes the same error (a necessary condition met, so the outcome follows), but it hedges with 'probably' where the original's conclusion is stated flatly. The matching conclusion type is in C.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Only if' marks a necessary condition: Advance -> Win. The original treats the met requirement as enough to guarantee the outcome. This choice has Reopen -> Pass inspection, the same move, and the same flat prediction.
explanations.D: Half right: it is a conditional error, but a different one. Hired -> Licensed, not Hired, so not Licensed denies the sufficient condition; the original affirms the necessary one.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the flaw is an unrepresentative sample, not a conditional error.

keyTakeaway: 'Only if' gives a requirement, not a guarantee; match the direction of the error, then the strength of the conclusion.
predictionHint: Requirement met, so outcome certain, in an 'only if' frame.

stimulus: The ferry runs only if the harbor is clear of ice. The harbor is not clear of ice today. Therefore, the ferry is not running today.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: The bridge is closed only if there is flooding upstream. There is flooding upstream today. Therefore, the bridge is closed today.
choices.B: The pool opens only if a lifeguard is on duty. The pool is not open today. Therefore, no lifeguard is on duty today.
choices.C: All of the museum's guides are certified. All certified guides know first aid. Therefore, all of the museum's guides know first aid.
choices.D: Both of the buses I happened to take this week during the busy morning commute were late. Therefore, most buses in the city run late on weekday mornings and evenings.
choices.E: Dried beans are safe to eat only if they have been boiled thoroughly. These beans have not been boiled thoroughly. Therefore, these beans are not safe to eat.

explanations.A: Necessary v. sufficient: the original denies the necessary condition; this one affirms it (flooding, so closed) and wrongly draws a conclusion. It is invalid.
explanations.B: Reversal: this denies the sufficient condition (not open, so no lifeguard). The original denies the necessary condition and concludes the sufficient one fails, which is valid.
explanations.C: Opposite structure: a chain of two universal rules is valid but has no 'only if' and no negative premise or conclusion.
explanations.D: Wrong part: this generalizes from a small sample. It has no conditional rule.
explanations.E: Correct. Ferry -> Clear; not Clear; so not Ferry. This runs Safe -> Boiled; not Boiled; so not Safe. Both deny the necessary condition and validly conclude the outcome fails.

keyTakeaway: In a valid 'only if' argument, failing the requirement proves the outcome fails.
predictionHint: X only if Y; not Y; so not X.

stimulus: Every certified welder at the shipyard has passed a vision test. Some of the shipyard's employees are certified welders. Therefore, some of the shipyard's employees have passed a vision test.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Some of the nurses on the ward are trained in pediatrics. Some people trained in pediatrics work nights. Therefore, some of the nurses work nights.
choices.B: All of the licensed pilots in the club have logged night-flying hours. Some of the club's members are licensed pilots. Therefore, some of the club's members have logged night-flying hours.
choices.C: Every lighthouse keeper on the coast is trained in signaling. Everyone trained in signaling can read semaphore. Therefore, every lighthouse keeper on the coast can read semaphore.
choices.D: Most of the orchestra's players are string players. Every string player has been tested for hearing loss. Therefore, most of the orchestra's players have been tested for hearing loss.
choices.E: Every economist at the firm reads the quarterly report. Every analyst at the firm reads the quarterly report. Therefore, some economists at the firm are analysts.

explanations.A: Wrong part: two 'some' premises do not combine; the overlap may be empty. The original has one universal premise, which is what makes it valid.
explanations.B: Correct. All Pilots -> Hours; some Members are Pilots; so some Members have Hours. One universal rule plus one 'some' premise gives a 'some' conclusion, exactly as in the original.
explanations.C: Half right: valid, but it chains two universal rules and concludes with 'every.' The original has a 'some' premise and a 'some' conclusion.
explanations.D: Half right: valid, but its premise and conclusion use 'most.' The original's quantifier is 'some.'
explanations.E: Shell game: two groups sharing a trait are assumed to overlap with each other. That is invalid, and the original is valid.

keyTakeaway: Match the quantifiers: one 'all' premise plus one 'some' premise yields 'some,' and the conclusion's quantifier must match too.
predictionHint: All B are C. Some A are B. So some A are C.

stimulus: The shipment was delayed either by customs or by the carrier. Customs records show that the shipment cleared on schedule. Therefore, the carrier delayed the shipment.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: The widespread outage on Elm Avenue last night was caused either by the storm or by a failed transformer. Inspectors confirmed that the transformer had indeed failed. Therefore, the storm did not cause the outage.
choices.B: If the sensor had failed, the alarm would have sounded. The alarm did not sound. Therefore, the sensor did not fail.
choices.C: The loaf failed to rise because of either the oven temperature or the yeast. The oven thermometer showed that the temperature was correct. Therefore, the yeast caused the loaf to fail to rise.
choices.D: The signal interference comes from the radar, the tower, or the substation. Engineers cleared the radar. Therefore, the interference comes from the tower or the substation.
choices.E: The painting is either a forgery or a lost original. Experts could not prove that it is a forgery. Therefore, it is a lost original.

explanations.A: Half right: it starts from two possible causes, but it confirms one and concludes the other is ruled out. The original rules one out and confirms the other.
explanations.B: Wrong part: this is a conditional argument. It is valid but has no list of alternatives to eliminate.
explanations.C: Correct. Two possible causes; one is eliminated; the other is concluded. Customs or Carrier; not Customs; so Carrier. This choice has Temperature or Yeast; not Temperature; so Yeast.
explanations.D: Half right: it eliminates one of three options but concludes only that one of the remaining two is the cause. The original narrows two options to one.
explanations.E: Wrong force: 'could not prove' is not the same as ruling out. The original's second premise is that customs cleared the shipment, a definite elimination.

keyTakeaway: Eliminating options only works when the other option is actually ruled out, not merely unproven.
predictionHint: Either X or Y; not X; so Y.

stimulus: Every proposal that includes a revenue forecast is subject to external audit. None of the proposals the board has approved is subject to external audit. Therefore, none of the proposals the board has approved includes a revenue forecast.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Every ship carrying hazardous cargo is subject to inspection at port. None of the ships in the northern fleet is subject to inspection at port. Therefore, none of the ships in the northern fleet carries hazardous cargo.
choices.B: None of the novels on the course syllabus is a work of nonfiction. None of the works of nonfiction in the library collection was written before 1900. Therefore, none of the novels on the syllabus was written before 1900.
choices.C: Some of the volunteers are lifeguards. No lifeguard is under sixteen. Therefore, some of the volunteers are not under sixteen.
choices.D: Every course in the honors track requires a thesis. Every course that requires a thesis carries four credits. Therefore, every course in the honors track carries four credits.
choices.E: None of the pilots in the training group has flown solo. Some of the instructors have flown solo. Therefore, none of the instructors is in the training group.

explanations.A: Correct. Forecast -> Audit; the board's proposals -> not Audit; so the board's proposals -> not Forecast. This choice has Hazardous -> Inspection; the northern fleet -> not Inspection; so the northern fleet -> not Hazardous. Same valid contrapositive chain, same 'none' conclusion.
explanations.B: Shell game: two 'none' premises do not combine. Novels and nonfiction share nothing, but that says nothing about novels and pre-1900 works. It is invalid.
explanations.C: Half right: valid, but one premise is 'some' and the conclusion is 'some are not.' The original is entirely universal, with a 'none' conclusion.
explanations.D: Wrong part: valid, but it chains two positive universal rules to a positive conclusion. It has no negative premise and no negative conclusion.
explanations.E: Extreme: the premises support only that some instructors are not in the training group. 'None' overreaches, so the argument is invalid.

keyTakeaway: 'All X are P' plus 'no Y are P' validly gives 'no Y are X'; check each choice for the same quantifiers and the same negative conclusion.
predictionHint: X -> P. Y -> not P. So Y -> not X.

stimulus: Archivist: The Orsolo ledger fragments show a systematic difference in letter formation between their earlier and later pages. Thus the fragments were probably written by at least two clerks. A household would seldom employ more than one clerk, whereas an institution commonly would. So the fragments were most likely kept by an institution.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: The Orsolo ledger fragments were probably written by at least two clerks.
choices.B: The Orsolo ledger fragments were kept by an institution.
choices.C: A household would seldom employ more than one clerk, whereas an institution commonly would.
choices.D: The Orsolo ledger fragments were most likely kept by an institution rather than by a household.
choices.E: A systematic difference in letter formation is a reliable sign that a document had more than one author.

explanations.A: This is the decoy "thus" claim: it is supported by the handwriting difference, but it is then used as a premise for the claim about who kept the fragments. It is a sub-conclusion, not the main conclusion.
explanations.B: Right topic, wrong force. The archivist says "most likely," and this choice drops the hedge and asserts certainty.
explanations.C: This is the bridging premise that links the number of clerks to the kind of keeper. It supports the conclusion; it is not what the argument is trying to establish.
explanations.D: Correct. The "thus" claim about two clerks is itself supported by the handwriting evidence and then used, with the claim about households and institutions, to reach the final "so" sentence. That last claim supports nothing further, and its hedge "most likely" is preserved.
explanations.E: This is an assumption the argument leans on, not something it states, and "reliable sign" is stronger than the archivist's "probably." The main conclusion is stated in the text, not implied by it.

keyTakeaway: A mid-stimulus "thus" can mark a sub-conclusion; the main conclusion is the claim that supports nothing further.
predictionHint: Follow the chain: handwriting, then two clerks, then institution. The last link is the point.

stimulus: Many commentators read the city's recent bond downgrade as a sign that its finances are collapsing. That reading is mistaken. The downgrade followed a change in the rating agency's methodology, which now penalizes every issuer carrying unfunded pension obligations, and over the same period the city's operating surplus grew in each of three consecutive years. A rating that moves with a methodology change while operating results improve is a poor indicator of an issuer's solvency.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: The city's operating surplus grew in each of three consecutive years.
choices.B: The city's bond downgrade is not a sign that its finances are collapsing.
choices.C: The city's finances are not collapsing.
choices.D: Many commentators regard the bond downgrade as a sign that the city's finances are collapsing.
choices.E: A rating that shifts when an agency changes its methodology is a poor indicator of an issuer's solvency.

explanations.A: This is evidence offered against the commentators' reading, not the point of the argument. Because-test: "The reading is mistaken because the surplus grew" works; the reverse does not.
explanations.B: Correct. The author states the position first ("That reading is mistaken") and spends the rest of the passage supporting it. The final sentence is a general reason, and the commentators' reading is the view being rejected.
explanations.C: The argument shows only that the downgrade is a poor indicator of collapse. Undermining the evidence for a claim does not establish that the claim is false; this choice overshoots.
explanations.D: This is the attributed view the author argues against. The author does not assert it.
explanations.E: This general claim is offered as a reason for the author's verdict on this city's downgrade. It supports the main conclusion rather than being it.

keyTakeaway: When the conclusion comes first and an opposing view is named, the conclusion rejects that view; match its exact scope, not a stronger one.
predictionHint: The downgrade is not good evidence of collapse; the author does not claim the finances are fine.

stimulus: Naturalist: It is true that the replanted stands on the cleared slopes are less diverse than the forests they replaced. But diversity is only a proxy for what we actually care about, which is whether a stand performs the functions of its predecessor: holding soil, filtering runoff, and sheltering native wildlife. Monitoring shows that every replanted stand more than ten years old performs all three. Hence the stands' lower diversity is no reason to count the replanting program a failure.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: The replanted stands are less diverse than the forests they replaced.
choices.B: The replanting program has succeeded in restoring the ecological functions of the original forests.
choices.C: Diversity is only a proxy for whether a stand performs the functions of its predecessor.
choices.D: Every replanted stand more than ten years old performs the functions of holding soil, filtering runoff, and sheltering native wildlife.
choices.E: The lower diversity of the replanted stands gives no reason to regard the replanting program as a failure.

explanations.A: This is the concession ("It is true that"). The naturalist grants it and then argues it does not matter; it is not the point being defended.
explanations.B: The monitoring covers only stands more than ten years old, and the conclusion is that low diversity is no reason to call the program a failure. Declaring a success is a stronger claim than the author makes.
explanations.C: This is a premise: it explains why low diversity is not the relevant measure. It supports the conclusion without being it.
explanations.D: This is the monitoring evidence. Because-test: "The low diversity is no reason to call it a failure because the stands perform these functions" reads naturally; reversed, it does not.
explanations.E: Correct. The opening concession grants the lower diversity, and the rest of the passage explains why that fact does not count against the program. "Hence" flags the claim the evidence supports and that supports nothing further.

keyTakeaway: A concession is granted and then answered; the main conclusion is what the author says follows despite it.
predictionHint: Low diversity does not count against the program; do not upgrade that to "the program succeeded."

stimulus: Critic: Some say that translating poetry is pointless because a translated poem inevitably loses the sound patterns of the original. But no one regards performing a piano transcription of an orchestral work as pointless on the grounds that it loses the orchestra's timbres. A transcription preserves a work's structure, and a translated poem preserves much of its imagery and argument. The loss of sound patterns, then, is no reason to consider the translation of poetry pointless.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: The inevitable loss of a poem's sound patterns in translation gives no reason to regard translating poetry as pointless.
choices.B: Translating poetry is a worthwhile activity.
choices.C: A translated poem preserves much of the imagery and argument of the original, even though its sound patterns are lost.
choices.D: Translating poetry is pointless because translations lose the sound patterns of the original.
choices.E: Piano transcriptions of orchestral works are not pointless even though they lose the orchestra's timbres.

explanations.A: Correct. The critic answers a specific objection and ends by saying that objection is "no reason." The analogy and the claim about what survives translation are both offered in support of that verdict.
explanations.B: The critic shows that one objection fails; this does not establish that translation is worthwhile. The claim goes beyond the scope of the conclusion.
explanations.C: This is a premise about what survives translation, used to support the verdict on the objection.
explanations.D: This is the view of "some" that the critic is arguing against.
explanations.E: This is the analogical premise. It is used to support the conclusion about poetry, which is the real subject of the argument.

keyTakeaway: Keep the conclusion at the author's scope: "this objection gives no reason" is weaker than "the opposite is true."
predictionHint: The loss of sound patterns is not a good reason to call poetry translation pointless.

stimulus: Sleep researcher: In each of the nine experiments we reviewed, the participants who slept at least eight hours before a memory test scored higher, on average, than the participants who slept less. Since the result was the same every time, it is certain that anyone who sleeps at least eight hours before a memory test will outperform anyone who sleeps less.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on nine experiments, a number too small to support any generalization about sleep
choices.B: assumes that eight hours is the best amount of sleep for improving memory performance
choices.C: draws a conclusion of certainty about every individual from evidence that supports, at most, a tendency among groups
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that participants who slept less did so because of stress that also impaired their memory
choices.E: takes for granted that all nine experiments used the same memory test

explanations.A: Nine consistent experiments can support a tendency; "any generalization" is an overstatement. The real problem is the strength of the conclusion, not the count.
explanations.B: The conclusion compares those who slept at least eight hours with those who slept less. It never claims eight is the best amount.
explanations.C: Correct. The evidence concerns group averages, and it makes a general tendency likely. The conclusion says "certain" and covers "anyone" compared with "anyone," which is far stronger than what the premises can deliver.
explanations.D: The conclusion is a prediction about who will score higher, not a claim about what causes the difference, so this alternative cause does not explain why the argument fails.
explanations.E: The argument needs only that each experiment found the same direction of result. Nothing in it depends on the tests being identical.

keyTakeaway: Check the force of the conclusion against the force of the premises; "certain" and "anyone" cannot come from averages.
predictionHint: Group averages, then a certainty claim about every individual.

stimulus: In an audit of the Hallam Library system's twelve branches, auditors found that every branch that extended its weekend hours saw its membership increase, and that no branch that left its weekend hours unchanged saw its membership increase. The audit also found that at exactly one branch, membership decreased.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The branch at which membership decreased did not extend its weekend hours.
choices.B: Extending weekend hours is an effective way for a branch to increase its membership.
choices.C: The branch at which membership decreased left its weekend hours unchanged.
choices.D: At least one of the twelve branches extended its weekend hours.
choices.E: Every branch that saw its membership increase had extended its weekend hours.

explanations.A: Correct. Every branch that extended its hours saw membership increase. A branch whose membership decreased did not increase, so it cannot be one that extended its hours. This follows from the facts with certainty.
explanations.B: The audit reports an association among branches; it says nothing about cause. A claim can be plausible in the world and still be unsupported by the information given.
explanations.C: The branch did not extend its hours, but it could have shortened them. "Left unchanged" is one of two possibilities, so it is not supported.
explanations.D: "Every branch that extended" is true even if none did. The statements do not guarantee that any branch extended its hours.
explanations.E: This reverses the conditional. A branch that shortened its hours is not covered by the findings, so an increase does not guarantee an extension.

keyTakeaway: Contrapositives are safe, converses are not; and "true in the world" is not the same as "supported by the passage."
predictionHint: Extended hours leads to an increase; a decrease therefore rules out extended hours, but not unchanged hours.

stimulus: Editorial: Most of the economists who reviewed the proposed pension reform judge it to be financially sustainable. Most of those same economists judge it to be fair to younger workers. It follows that most of the economists who reviewed the reform judge it to be both financially sustainable and fair to younger workers.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: infers that every reviewer holds both judgments from the premise that most reviewers hold each judgment
choices.B: treats the judgments of the reviewing economists as sufficient to establish that the reform is actually both sustainable and fair to younger workers
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that some reviewers judge the reform to be neither sustainable nor fair
choices.D: infers that at least some reviewers hold both judgments from the premise that most reviewers hold each judgment
choices.E: infers that most of a group hold two judgments together from the premise that most hold each separately

explanations.A: The conclusion is about "most," not "every." This describes a different, stronger inference than the one made.
explanations.B: The conclusion reports what the economists judge, not whether the reform actually is sustainable and fair, so no such leap is made.
explanations.C: That possibility is compatible with both premises and does not bear on whether "most" hold the two judgments together.
explanations.D: That inference would be valid, since two majorities of one group must overlap, and it is not what the editorial does. The editorial concludes "most," not "some."
explanations.E: Correct. Two majorities must overlap, which guarantees only that some reviewers hold both judgments. The editorial concludes that most do, which is stronger than "most" plus "most" can support, since the two majorities may largely miss each other.

keyTakeaway: "Most A are B" plus "most A are C" guarantees only that some A are both B and C.
predictionHint: Two separate majorities do not add up to a majority holding both views.

stimulus: The Brenner archive's catalogue records the ink used in every manuscript it holds. Every manuscript in the archive is written in iron-gall ink, carbon ink, or both. All of the archive's carbon-ink manuscripts date from 1700 or later. Most of its iron-gall manuscripts date from before 1700.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most of the manuscripts held in the Brenner archive, taken as a whole and whatever their ink, date from before 1700.
choices.B: Some of the archive's iron-gall manuscripts date from 1700 or later.
choices.C: Every manuscript in the archive that dates from before 1700 is written in iron-gall ink.
choices.D: The iron-gall manuscripts in the archive are, on average, older than the carbon-ink manuscripts.
choices.E: The archive contains fewer carbon-ink manuscripts than iron-gall manuscripts.

explanations.A: The "most" claim covers only the iron-gall manuscripts. The archive could hold many carbon-ink manuscripts, all from 1700 or later, outnumbering the older ones.
explanations.B: "Most" leaves open that all of them predate 1700. Nothing guarantees any exceptions.
explanations.C: Correct. A manuscript from before 1700 cannot be carbon ink, since all carbon-ink manuscripts are from 1700 or later. Every manuscript uses iron-gall, carbon, or both, so a pre-1700 manuscript must use iron-gall. The "most" claim is not needed.
explanations.D: A majority being older does not fix an average age: a few very recent iron-gall manuscripts could pull the average below that of the carbon-ink ones. "Most" is a count, not an average.
explanations.E: The passage gives no information about the relative numbers of the two kinds of ink.

keyTakeaway: Valid conclusions come from the "all" statements; a "most" statement is usually bait for a stronger claim.
predictionHint: Before 1700 rules out carbon ink; every manuscript has at least one of the two inks.

stimulus: Naturalist: Frog numbers in the marsh have halved since the drainage channel was dug, and the losses were concentrated in the ponds nearest the channel. The channel is therefore probably responsible for the decline. Because it was built solely to serve the new housing development, the development's backers should fund restoration of the ponds.
stem: The claim that the drainage channel is probably responsible for the decline in frog numbers plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the evidence about where the losses of frogs were concentrated in the marsh.
choices.B: It is an intermediate conclusion that is supported by evidence and that, together with another claim, supports the main conclusion.
choices.C: It is evidence offered in support of the claim that frog numbers in the marsh have halved.
choices.D: It is a view held by the development's backers that the argument attempts to refute.
choices.E: It is background information that introduces the topic, with nothing offered for or against it.

explanations.A: The argument does not stop here: the claim is used to support the recommendation that the development's backers fund restoration, which is the main conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. The claim follows from the evidence about where the losses were concentrated ("therefore"), and it is then used, with the fact that the channel was built for the development, to reach the recommendation about funding.
explanations.C: This reverses the direction of support. The halving of the frog numbers is the evidence; the claim about the channel is drawn from it.
explanations.D: Nothing attributes the claim to the backers, and the naturalist asserts it rather than opposing it.
explanations.E: The claim has support (the loss pattern) and itself supports a further claim, so it is not mere context.

keyTakeaway: Ask two questions: is it supported, and does it support something further? Yes to both marks a sub-conclusion.
predictionHint: A "therefore" claim that is then used again is the hinge of a two-step argument.

stimulus: Of course, the tolling system will cost the city several million dollars to install, and some commuters will pay more than they do now. But the revenue it raises will fund bus lines that carry more commuters per hour than the highway lanes it charges for. And because those bus riders would otherwise add to the traffic, even drivers who pay tolls end up with faster trips. So the city should adopt the system.
stem: The claim that some commuters will pay more than they do now plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is evidence offered in direct support of the claim that the city should adopt the system.
choices.B: It is a claim that the argument attempts to show is false.
choices.C: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from the claim about the bus lines.
choices.D: It is an unfavorable consideration that the argument grants and then argues is outweighed.
choices.E: It is background information that the argument neither accepts nor responds to.

explanations.A: The claim counts against adoption. The argument cites it only to answer it, so it does not support the conclusion.
explanations.B: The argument never denies it. It concedes the point and argues that other considerations outweigh it, which is different from rebutting it.
explanations.C: The bus-line claims are offered against this consideration, not as a basis for it. Nothing in the argument derives it.
explanations.D: Correct. "Of course" signals a concession. The argument accepts that some commuters will pay more, and then the "But" and "even drivers who pay tolls" sentences answer it without denying it.
explanations.E: The argument responds to it directly: the "But" sentence and the "even drivers who pay tolls" clause are aimed at it.

keyTakeaway: A concession is accepted and then outweighed; a rejected view is denied. The difference is whether the author grants the claim.
predictionHint: "Of course" followed by "But" marks a point granted and then answered.

stimulus: Many economists expect the new fuel tax to raise the price of freight. Since higher freight prices push shippers toward rail, the tax is likely to shift cargo from highways to rail. A shift of that kind would reduce highway wear. So the tax will probably bring a benefit that its critics have overlooked.
stem: The claim that many economists expect the new fuel tax to raise the price of freight plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is a claim that the argument accepts and uses, together with another claim, to support an intermediate conclusion.
choices.B: It is a position that the argument as a whole is directed against.
choices.C: It is a consideration that the argument grants but then treats as outweighed.
choices.D: It is the intermediate conclusion from which the main conclusion is drawn.
choices.E: It is evidence offered directly for the claim that the tax will bring a benefit its critics have overlooked.

explanations.A: Correct. The argument builds on the expectation: "Since higher freight prices push shippers toward rail" leads to the claim that cargo will shift to rail. That shift is an intermediate step toward the final benefit claim.
explanations.B: The attribution to "many economists" looks like a view to be rejected, but the argument relies on it. The critics who overlooked a benefit are not said to be the economists.
explanations.C: A concession supports nothing and is answered. This claim is used as a premise in the next step, not answered.
explanations.D: The intermediate conclusion is the claim that cargo is likely to shift from highways to rail. The economists' expectation is a premise supporting it.
explanations.E: It supports the shift to rail first, and only through that claim and the claim about highway wear does it bear on the final benefit. "Directly" is the word that fails.

keyTakeaway: An attributed view is a premise if the author builds on it, and context only if the author argues against or around it.
predictionHint: Does the author use the economists' expectation as a reason, or answer it?

stimulus: Enrollment at the village school did shrink steadily, and it is tempting to conclude that the shrinkage explains the school's closure. Yet enrollment had been shrinking for a decade while the district kept the school open, and two schools in the district with smaller enrollments remain open today. The closure must instead have been prompted by the school's failed roof inspection last spring.
stem: The claim that the shrinkage of enrollment explains the closure of the village school plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the facts about the district's other schools are meant to support.
choices.B: It is a consideration that the argument grants as true but treats as outweighed by other factors.
choices.C: It is a view that the argument opposes and that the cited facts about the district are used to undermine.
choices.D: It is an intermediate conclusion that, together with the history of the district, supports the claim about the roof inspection.
choices.E: It is a premise that the argument accepts and uses to support the claim that the roof inspection prompted the closure.

explanations.A: The facts about the district are used against this claim. The main conclusion is the final sentence about the roof inspection.
explanations.B: The author grants that enrollment shrank, but not that this explains the closure. The explanation is rejected, not outweighed.
explanations.C: Correct. The "Yet" sentence presents a decade of shrinkage without closure and smaller schools staying open, both aimed against this explanation. The author concludes that a different cause "instead" prompted the closure.
explanations.D: Nothing leads from this claim to the roof inspection; the inspection claim is reached by eliminating this explanation, not by building on it.
explanations.E: The argument does not accept this explanation. It accepts only that enrollment shrank, which is a different claim from the one in the stem.

keyTakeaway: Separate the fact conceded from the explanation rejected; the role of a claim depends on its exact wording.
predictionHint: "Tempting to conclude… Yet…" introduces a view the author will take apart.

stimulus:
Lobbyist: Public libraries reduce what people spend on books, which hurts publishers. The government should therefore stop funding public libraries.

Senator: By that reasoning, the government should also close public parks, since parks reduce what people spend on gym memberships, and public schools, since they reduce what people spend on private tutoring.
stem: The senator responds to the lobbyist by

choices.A: disputing the factual claim that public libraries reduce what people spend on books
choices.B: citing instances that conflict with a universal claim the lobbyist has explicitly stated
choices.C: arguing that libraries provide benefits to the public that outweigh whatever harm is done to publishers by reduced book sales
choices.D: extending the lobbyist's line of reasoning to further cases in which it would yield implausible conclusions
choices.E: demonstrating that the lobbyist's conclusion is false

explanations.A: The senator never questions the lobbyist's premise. The response is aimed at the inference drawn from it.
explanations.B: A counterexample targets a stated universal claim. The lobbyist states none, only a claim about libraries and an inference, so the referent fails on "explicitly stated."
explanations.C: The senator mentions no benefits of libraries and weighs nothing against the harm to publishers.
explanations.D: Correct. "By that reasoning" refers to the lobbyist's inference (harm to an industry, so stop funding). The parks and schools are further cases to which that inference applies, and the conclusions it yields there are presented as unacceptable.
explanations.E: The senator suggests the reasoning goes too far but does not demonstrate that the conclusion is false; a flawed argument can still have a true conclusion.

keyTakeaway: In a method question, check every noun against the text: "a universal claim the speaker stated" must actually appear.
predictionHint: Applies the same reasoning to parallel cases to show it proves too much.

stimulus: Alder Quay lies on the coast, at the mouth of the Pell River. The flood agency claims that restoring the wetlands upstream of Alder Quay will protect the town from flooding. The town's flooding, however, comes solely from storm surges that arrive from the sea. The agency's claim is therefore mistaken, since ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: wetlands located upstream of a town can protect it from flooding that is caused by water arriving from upstream
choices.B: wetlands located upstream of a town can protect it only from flooding caused by water arriving from upstream
choices.C: storm surges from the sea have become more frequent in recent decades
choices.D: sea walls and similar coastal structures can protect a town from the storm surges that arrive from the sea
choices.E: restoring wetlands is more expensive than building defenses against storm surges

explanations.A: This says what upstream wetlands can do, not what they cannot do. Without "only," it leaves open that they also help against surges from the sea, so the conclusion does not follow.
explanations.B: Correct. The blank follows "since," so it must be the premise that makes the conclusion follow. If upstream wetlands help only against upstream-caused flooding, and Alder Quay's flooding comes solely from the sea, the wetlands cannot protect the town.
explanations.C: More frequent surges make flooding worse, but they say nothing about whether upstream wetlands could stop it.
explanations.D: Other measures may work, but this does not show that the wetlands will fail. It is a different question from the one the agency raised.
explanations.E: The conclusion is about whether the wetlands will protect the town, not about the cost of options. Cost is a different dimension.

keyTakeaway: After "since," supply the bridge; a "can" version of a bridge is the trap for the "can only" version that actually closes the gap.
predictionHint: Wetlands help only with upstream water; the flooding is all from the sea.

stimulus: Admittedly, translated novels have won the Kessler Prize fewer times than novels originally written in English. But translated novels make up only a small share of the entries submitted, and the share of submitted novels that go on to win is the same for translated novels as for those originally written in English. Therefore, ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: the judges treat translated entries less favorably than entries originally written in English
choices.B: the prize's judging process is entirely free of bias
choices.C: translated novels are, on average, no less accomplished than novels originally written in English
choices.D: translated novels make up only a small share of the novels that have been submitted to the Kessler Prize over the years
choices.E: the smaller number of prizes won by translated novels does not indicate that the judges treat translated entries less favorably

explanations.A: The equal share of entries that win points the other way. This is the inference the argument is meant to block.
explanations.B: Equal win rates show that the lower count is not evidence of bias against translations. They do not prove the process is free of every kind of bias.
explanations.C: The facts concern entries and wins, not literary quality. Nothing in the passage measures how accomplished the novels are.
explanations.D: This restates a premise. A completion that repeats a fact already given does not draw a conclusion from it.
explanations.E: Correct. The blank follows "Therefore," so it is a modest conclusion. The concession is the lower number of wins; the "But" sentence explains it by the small number of entries, with equal win rates. The conclusion is that the count alone does not show unfavorable treatment.

keyTakeaway: After a concession and a rebuttal, complete with the modest conclusion the rebuttal licenses, not a stronger one.
predictionHint: Fewer wins reflect fewer entries; they do not show that judges disfavor translations.

stimulus: The Dunmore school district's test scores rose by an average of six points in the year after it adopted a new reading curriculum. Over the same year, scores in the neighboring districts, which are similar to Dunmore in student population and which did not adopt the curriculum, rose by an average of six points as well. So the curriculum was not responsible for any of Dunmore's rise, since ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: any contribution by the curriculum would have put Dunmore's scores ahead of those of similar districts that lacked it
choices.B: a rise in a district's scores can be caused by factors that have nothing to do with the reading curriculum it uses
choices.C: some factor affecting every district in the region raised scores in each of them
choices.D: districts elsewhere that adopted the new curriculum also saw their scores rise by about six points
choices.E: Dunmore's scores rose by an average of six points in the year after the curriculum was adopted

explanations.A: Correct. The blank follows "since," so it is the premise that makes the stated conclusion follow. If any contribution from the curriculum would have put Dunmore ahead of similar districts, equal rises show there was none.
explanations.B: That other causes are possible does not show the curriculum contributed nothing; Dunmore's rise could have had both.
explanations.C: A shared factor could explain the neighbors' rise, but it would not exclude a further boost from the curriculum. Only the claim that any contribution would show up as a larger rise closes that gap.
explanations.D: This is about other districts. It does not compare similar districts with and without the curriculum, so it cannot show the curriculum made no difference.
explanations.E: This restates the first premise and adds nothing that connects equal rises to the lack of a contribution.

keyTakeaway: After "since," ask what would have to be true for the evidence to rule out the cause; a possible alternative cause is not enough.
predictionHint: If the curriculum had added anything, Dunmore would have pulled ahead of its peers.

stimulus: Heritage officer: Every one of the thirty-one timber bridges that still stand in the Calder Valley and date from before 1850 rests on stone footings. Clearly, stone footings were the standard way of building timber bridges in the Calder Valley before 1850.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: concludes that stone footings account for the bridges' survival from the mere fact that the two go together
choices.B: infers a property of each bridge from a property of its footings, ignoring how footings and timber interact
choices.C: generalizes about a whole class from members that may have survived because they had the feature in question
choices.D: assumes that timber bridges built outside the valley before 1850 were built the same way as those inside it
choices.E: treats the great age of the surviving bridges as evidence of the quality of their builders' craftsmanship

explanations.A: Shell game: the conclusion is about what was standard practice, not about what caused the bridges to survive. The officer never claims footings explain survival.
explanations.B: Wrong part: nothing in the argument moves from properties of footings to properties of bridges; the claim is about how many bridges had stone footings.
explanations.C: Correct. The only bridges examined are ones that still stand. If stone footings helped bridges last, survivors would have them even if many bridges of the period did not, so the sample is skewed on the very feature at issue.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the conclusion is limited to the Calder Valley, so bridges elsewhere are irrelevant.
explanations.E: Out of scope: craftsmanship and quality play no role in the argument.

keyTakeaway: When every member of a sample has survived, ask whether surviving could depend on the very property being generalized.
predictionHint: Only survivors were checked, and the feature may be why they survived.

stimulus: Economic adviser: Over the past decade, the combined output of Veldmark's industries has grown more slowly than the combined output of neighboring Orsett's industries. So we can be sure that every one of Veldmark's industries has grown more slowly than the corresponding Orsett industry.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: treats a difference in growth rates between two economies as though it were a difference in their absolute size
choices.B: compares two economies without establishing that Orsett's industries resemble those of other neighboring countries
choices.C: concludes that Veldmark's slower growth is explained by its industrial policies when other factors may account for it
choices.D: draws a conclusion about how Veldmark's industries will fare in the future from how they fared in the past decade
choices.E: infers that a relation between two wholes holds between each pair of their corresponding parts

explanations.A: Comparison shift: the premise compares rates and so does the conclusion; neither mentions absolute size.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns Orsett itself, not other countries, so whether Orsett is typical does not matter.
explanations.C: Shell game: the adviser offers no explanation of Veldmark's growth, causal or otherwise.
explanations.D: Out of scope: both premise and conclusion are about the past decade, so no prediction is made.
explanations.E: Correct. The premise compares the two economies as wholes. The conclusion needs the comparison to hold industry by industry, but a slower total is compatible with some Veldmark industries outpacing their Orsett counterparts.

keyTakeaway: A relation that holds between two wholes need not hold between each pair of corresponding parts.
predictionHint: Total beats total, so every part beats its counterpart: whole-to-part.

stimulus: Archivist: The letter was written by Corvin Hale. Its script matches the library's reference specimen of Hale's handwriting, and that specimen is known to be Hale's because it was authenticated years ago by comparison with this very letter.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: infers that the letter is old from the fact that the specimen was authenticated years ago
choices.B: relies on a premise whose own support depends on the truth of the conclusion it is offered to establish
choices.C: assumes that the reference specimen is the only surviving example of Hale's handwriting
choices.D: accepts without question that the library's records of the specimen's authentication are accurate
choices.E: draws a conclusion about every document in the library's collection from the status of one specimen

explanations.A: Out of scope: the argument is about who wrote the letter, not when it was written.
explanations.B: Correct. The match to the specimen supports Hale's authorship only if the specimen is Hale's, and the specimen was certified by comparison with the letter, which presupposes that the letter is Hale's.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the argument does not assume the specimen is unique; other examples would not remove the circularity.
explanations.D: Wrong part: this attacks the reliability of a premise rather than the inference; accurate records would still leave the circle intact.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns a single letter, not the collection.

keyTakeaway: If a premise could be established only by first assuming the conclusion, the argument is circular.
predictionHint: The specimen vouches for the letter, and the letter vouched for the specimen.

stimulus: Mayor Ortiz claims that the new bridge is structurally unsafe. But Ortiz's family owns the ferry company that would lose business if the bridge opened. Therefore, the bridge must be safe.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: assumes that only a licensed engineer is in a position to judge whether a bridge is safe
choices.B: generalizes about all owners of ferry companies from the behavior of one family
choices.C: concludes that the bridge will be profitable from the claim that it is safe
choices.D: rejects a claim because of its source's personal stake rather than on its merits
choices.E: takes the absence of proof that the bridge is unsafe as proof that it is safe

explanations.A: Out of scope: the argument never says who is qualified to judge safety.
explanations.B: Out of scope: Ortiz's family is the only ferry owner mentioned, and no claim about ferry owners in general is made.
explanations.C: Out of scope: profit is never discussed.
explanations.D: Correct. The only reason given for rejecting Ortiz's claim is Ortiz's financial interest, which does not show that the claim is false.
explanations.E: Shell game: the argument does not discuss proof or its absence; it discredits the person making the claim.

keyTakeaway: A source's motives are not evidence that the source's claim is false.
predictionHint: Attacks the speaker's interest, not the safety claim.

stimulus: Race official: To qualify for the regional final, a runner must complete a sanctioned qualifying race in under forty minutes. Dana completed a sanctioned qualifying race in thirty-eight minutes, so Dana will qualify for the regional final.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: treats something required for an outcome as though it were enough to guarantee the outcome
choices.B: treats something sufficient for an outcome as though it were required for the outcome
choices.C: generalizes about all runners from the performance of a single runner
choices.D: accepts the official's statement of the rule without any independent confirmation
choices.E: assumes that Dana is faster than every other runner who has attempted to qualify
