explanations.A: Correct. Finishing under forty minutes is stated as a requirement. The argument treats meeting the requirement as ensuring qualification, though other conditions could also be needed.
explanations.B: Reversal: this describes the opposite error. The argument never says that finishing under forty minutes is the only way to qualify.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the conclusion is about Dana alone.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the rule is offered as a premise, and doubting it is not the argument's flaw.
explanations.E: Out of scope: no comparison with other runners is made.

keyTakeaway: A stated requirement tells you what is necessary, not that meeting it is enough.
predictionHint: Required becomes guaranteed.

stimulus: Local reporter: The share of Marlow's residents who attend the municipal symphony fell from 12 percent ten years ago to 9 percent today. So fewer Marlow residents attend the symphony now than did ten years ago.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: infers that the symphony's quality has declined from the fact that fewer residents attend it
choices.B: draws a conclusion about all municipal arts organizations from the case of one symphony
choices.C: treats a decline in a proportion as though it were a decline in the corresponding number
choices.D: assumes that attendance is the best measure of a symphony's success
choices.E: confuses the cause of the decline in attendance with its effect

explanations.A: Out of scope: the argument says nothing about quality.
explanations.B: Out of scope: only one symphony is discussed.
explanations.C: Correct. If Marlow's population grew enough, a smaller share could still be a larger number of attendees.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the argument does not evaluate success, only attendance.
explanations.E: Out of scope: no cause is asserted at all.

keyTakeaway: A falling percentage does not guarantee a falling count; ask what happened to the total.
predictionHint: Share fell, so count fell: percent to number.

stimulus: Every branch of the Harlow Public Library other than the Eastgate branch offers evening hours. Free tutoring is offered only at branches that offer evening hours. The Eastgate branch runs a free tutoring program.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: The Eastgate branch is the only branch that offers free tutoring.
choices.B: Every branch of the Harlow Public Library offers evening hours.
choices.C: The Eastgate branch is the only branch that does not offer evening hours.
choices.D: At least one branch that offers evening hours does not offer free tutoring.
choices.E: Every branch other than the Eastgate branch offers free tutoring.

explanations.A: Extreme: the statements say nothing that rules out tutoring at other branches.
explanations.B: Correct. Tutoring requires evening hours, and Eastgate offers tutoring, so Eastgate offers evening hours. 'Other than Eastgate' only exempted Eastgate from the first claim; it did not say Eastgate lacks evening hours. Every branch therefore offers them.
explanations.C: Opposite: Eastgate's tutoring program requires that it offers evening hours, so it is not an exception.
explanations.D: Wrong force: 'only at' makes evening hours necessary for tutoring, not sufficient, but that does not show that any branch actually lacks tutoring.
explanations.E: Reversal: this turns 'tutoring only where there are evening hours' into 'evening hours guarantee tutoring'.

keyTakeaway: 'Other than X' sets X aside without saying anything about X; 'only at' names a requirement, not a guarantee.
predictionHint: Tutoring requires evening hours, so Eastgate has them too.

stimulus: At the Larkspur shelter, most of the volunteers who completed the orientation and had volunteered elsewhere before are still active, whereas most of the volunteers who completed the orientation but had not volunteered elsewhere before have left. Every volunteer who did not complete the orientation has left.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most volunteers who had volunteered elsewhere before are still active.
choices.B: Most volunteers who completed the orientation are still active.
choices.C: Volunteers who had not volunteered elsewhere before are more likely to leave than those who had.
choices.D: No volunteer who is still active skipped the orientation.
choices.E: Some volunteers who completed the orientation and had volunteered elsewhere before have left.

explanations.A: Wrong part: the 'most' claim is limited to experienced volunteers who also completed the orientation. Experienced volunteers who skipped it have all left, and their number is unknown.
explanations.B: Wrong part: 'most' applies only within each subgroup of orientation completers; the sizes of the subgroups are unknown, and the other subgroup mostly left.
explanations.C: Extreme: the contrast holds among orientation completers only. Overall rates also depend on how many volunteers skipped the orientation.
explanations.D: Correct. Every volunteer who skipped the orientation has left, so anyone still active must have completed it.
explanations.E: Wrong force: 'most' are still active is compatible with all of them being active.

keyTakeaway: Keep every modifier attached: a claim about 'those who did X and Y' is not a claim about 'those who did Y'.
predictionHint: Everyone who skipped the orientation is gone, so the active ones all completed it.

stimulus: An internal review audited a firm's invoices and its expense claims, in that order, and found improper documentation in 4 percent and 9 percent of the items audited, respectively. The audit that found the higher percentage examined 600 items; the other audit examined 1,000 items.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: More expense claims than invoices were found to be improperly documented.
choices.B: More invoices than expense claims were found to be improperly documented.
choices.C: At least half of the improperly documented items found by the two audits were invoices.
choices.D: The invoice audit examined fewer items than the expense claim audit did.
choices.E: The expense claim audit found the higher percentage only because it examined fewer items.

explanations.A: Correct. 'Respectively' pairs 4 percent with invoices and 9 percent with expense claims. The expense claim audit found the higher percentage, so it examined 600 items: 54 problem items. The invoice audit examined 1,000 items: 40 problem items.
explanations.B: Reversal: this follows only if the percentages are paired with the wrong audits.
explanations.C: Extreme: 40 of 94 improperly documented items were invoices, which is under half.
explanations.D: Shell game: this too holds only if 'respectively' is misapplied; the invoice audit examined 1,000 items.
explanations.E: Out of scope: nothing says why the percentages differ.

keyTakeaway: With 'respectively', match the lists position by position before doing any arithmetic.
predictionHint: Pair 4 percent with invoices and 9 percent with claims, then compute 54 versus 40.

stimulus: Port records show that it was not uncommon for ships to be held in harbor by storms for more than a week. No ship, however, was ever held in harbor for more than a month.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most ships that entered the port were held in harbor by storms for more than a week.
choices.B: Some ships were held in harbor by storms for nearly a full month.
choices.C: Storms were the most frequent reason that ships were held in harbor at the port.
choices.D: Every ship that was held in harbor by storms was held for at least a week.
choices.E: At least some ships were held in harbor by storms for more than a week.

explanations.A: Extreme: 'not uncommon' means it happened fairly often, not that most ships were affected.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the records rule out stays beyond a month but say nothing about stays that came close to it.
explanations.C: Out of scope: nothing compares storms with other causes of delay.
explanations.D: Extreme: some storm delays were over a week, but nothing says all were.
explanations.E: Correct. 'Not uncommon' translates to 'it happened, and not rarely', so at least some ships were held for over a week.

keyTakeaway: A double negative like 'not uncommon' simply means it happens; translate it before comparing choices.
predictionHint: Not uncommon means some did.

stimulus: Critics claim that the planned reservoir will devastate the region's trout population. The state wildlife agency reports, however, that trout counts have held steady in each of the five comparable reservoirs it has monitored since they were built.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The planned reservoir will leave the region's trout population exactly as large as it is today.
choices.B: The agency's findings give some reason to doubt the critics' claim.
choices.C: The critics have not studied any of the reservoirs that the agency has monitored.
choices.D: Trout counts in the planned reservoir will hold steady, as they have in the five monitored reservoirs.
choices.E: The five reservoirs the agency has monitored are the only comparable reservoirs in the region.

explanations.A: Extreme: the agency reports on other reservoirs, so no certainty about the planned one follows.
explanations.B: Correct. The critics' claim is attributed to them, and the agency's data on comparable reservoirs cut against it, which gives modest reason for doubt.
explanations.C: Out of scope: nothing is said about the critics' research.
explanations.D: Extreme: results at comparable reservoirs do not guarantee the same result at this one.
explanations.E: Out of scope: 'each of the five it has monitored' leaves open that other comparable reservoirs exist.

keyTakeaway: A claim attributed to critics is not the author's claim; evidence against it supports doubt, not its opposite.
predictionHint: The agency's data cut against the critics, modestly.

stimulus: The Riverside Chess Club's rules state that unless a member has paid the annual dues, she may not vote in the club's elections. Mara, a member, voted in this year's election, and no rule was broken.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Every member who has paid the annual dues voted in this year's election.
choices.B: Mara was the only member who voted in this year's election.
choices.C: Mara paid the annual dues.
choices.D: Mara has belonged to the club for more than a year.
choices.E: Mara paid her dues earlier than most members paid theirs.

explanations.A: Necessary v. sufficient: paying dues is required for voting, so it does not follow that everyone who paid actually voted.
explanations.B: Extreme: nothing limits the number of voters.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Unless' introduces a requirement: no dues, no vote. Mara voted without breaking a rule, so she paid.
explanations.D: Out of scope: length of membership is never mentioned.
explanations.E: Comparison shift: nothing is said about when anyone paid.

keyTakeaway: 'Unless' marks a requirement: no dues, no vote means vote implies dues.
predictionHint: Mara voted lawfully, so she must have paid.

stimulus: Although studies consistently link lifelong bilingualism to a later onset of dementia symptoms, it would be premature to conclude that learning a second language in adulthood will delay those symptoms, since most of the bilingual participants in these studies acquired both of their languages in early childhood.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The studies leave open whether learning a second language in adulthood delays dementia symptoms.
choices.B: Learning a second language in adulthood has no effect on the age at which dementia symptoms begin.
choices.C: Learning a second language in adulthood protects against dementia less well than learning one in early childhood.
choices.D: Acquiring two languages in early childhood brings about a later onset of dementia symptoms.
choices.E: Most people who learn a second language in adulthood develop dementia symptoms later than monolinguals do.

explanations.A: Correct. 'Premature to conclude' translates to 'not yet shown'. Because most participants were early bilinguals, the studies give little evidence about adult learners.
explanations.B: Opposite: 'premature to conclude that it will delay' says the effect is unproven, not that it is absent.
explanations.C: Comparison shift: no comparison between adult and childhood learning is supported.
explanations.D: Wrong force: the studies are said to 'link' bilingualism to later onset, which is not stated as causation.
explanations.E: Opposite: this asserts the very conclusion the passage calls premature.

keyTakeaway: 'Premature to conclude X' means X is unproven, not that X is false.
predictionHint: Unproven for adult learners, not disproven.

stimulus: Proponents of the zoning change insist that it will not raise rents. The city's own housing data, however, show that rents rose in every district where a comparable change was adopted, though never by more than ten percent in a year.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The zoning change will raise rents by less than ten percent in its first year.
choices.B: Proponents of the zoning change have misrepresented the city's own housing data to the public.
choices.C: Rents in a district will rise only if a change like this one is adopted in that district.
choices.D: What happened in districts with comparable changes runs counter to the proponents' claim.
choices.E: Rents rose in every district because of the comparable zoning changes adopted there.

explanations.A: Extreme: the data concern other districts, so a prediction for this district, with a number, goes beyond them.
explanations.B: Shell game: the proponents' claim is attributed to them, and nothing says they knew of or distorted the data.
explanations.C: Necessary v. sufficient: the data show rents rising after such changes, not that such changes are the only cause of rises.
explanations.D: Correct. Proponents say no rent increase; in comparable districts rents rose. The data do not settle the case but run against the claim.
explanations.E: Wrong force: the data show rents rose where changes were adopted, not that the changes caused the rise.

keyTakeaway: Keep attributed claims attributed: evidence against what proponents say supports doubt about their claim, not a precise prediction.
predictionHint: Comparable cases cut against the proponents.

stimulus: No contractor who has not filed a lien waiver is paid unless the owner has signed off in writing. Every contractor on the Alder Street project was paid, yet the owner signed off in writing on none of their invoices.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Every contractor who filed a lien waiver was paid.
choices.B: The owner refused to sign off on any of the Alder Street invoices.
choices.C: No contractor on any other project was paid without having filed a lien waiver.
choices.D: Some contractor on the Alder Street project was paid without having filed a lien waiver.
choices.E: Every contractor on the Alder Street project filed a lien waiver.

explanations.A: Necessary v. sufficient: a waiver is part of what lets a contractor be paid without sign-off, but filing does not guarantee payment.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the owner may simply never have been asked; 'did not sign' is not 'refused'.
explanations.C: Out of scope: other projects are not described, and the rule may not apply there.
explanations.D: Opposite: with no written sign-off, a contractor who was paid cannot be a non-filer.
explanations.E: Correct. Translate: a contractor with no waiver and no sign-off is not paid. Alder contractors were paid and had no sign-off, so each filed a waiver.

keyTakeaway: Unpack 'no X unless Y' into 'X and not Y means not paid' before testing each choice.
predictionHint: Paid with no sign-off means the waiver was filed.

stimulus: Librarian: Since the Dunmore Public Library began sending patrons text-message reminders a few days before their books are due, the share of books returned late has fallen from 22 percent to 9 percent. The reminders clearly deserve the credit for this improvement.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the library raised its late fines at about the time it began sending the reminders
choices.B: Whether most patrons find text-message reminders more convenient than other kinds of reminders
choices.C: Whether the library's circulation records were kept accurately before the reminders began
choices.D: Whether other libraries in the region have also begun sending reminders to their patrons in recent years
choices.E: Whether the library spent more on setting up the reminder system than it collected in late fees last year

explanations.A: Correct. If fines rose at the same time, the higher cost of lateness could explain the improvement and the reminders lose credit; if nothing else changed, the reminders are the likely cause. The answers swing the conclusion in opposite directions.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: convenience does not bear on whether the reminders, rather than something else, produced the drop. Either answer leaves the causal claim where it was.
explanations.C: Premise booster: this questions the accuracy of the data the argument takes as given. Evaluate tests the step from evidence to conclusion, not the evidence itself.
explanations.D: Out of scope: what other libraries are doing says nothing about why late returns fell at Dunmore.
explanations.E: Comparison shift: cost against fee revenue concerns whether the program pays for itself, not whether it caused the improvement.

keyTakeaway: For a causal claim, ask about the most obvious simultaneous change; if Yes weakens and No strengthens, you have the answer.
predictionHint: Did anything else change at the same time that could explain fewer late returns?

stimulus: Mayor: A survey of people leaving the Harbor Street farmers market found that 80 percent of them favor building a new parking garage near downtown. So a large majority of the city's residents favor building the garage.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the new garage would be paid for entirely with public money
choices.B: Whether the survey's 80 percent figure was calculated correctly from the responses collected
choices.C: Whether market shoppers drive downtown more often than residents generally do
choices.D: Whether the garage would be larger than any other parking structure in the city
choices.E: Whether the farmers market has been held at the same location for more than ten years

explanations.A: Out of scope: how the garage is funded is not part of the claim about how many residents favor it.
explanations.B: Premise booster: this challenges the arithmetic of the survey result, which the argument takes as given.
explanations.C: Correct. If market shoppers drive downtown more than residents in general, the sample is skewed toward people who want parking and the conclusion is weakened; if they do not, the sample looks more representative.
explanations.D: Comparison shift: the garage's relative size has no bearing on whether residents favor it.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: how long the market has been in place leaves the question of who was surveyed untouched.

keyTakeaway: When a sample is the premise, evaluate whether the people sampled differ from the target group in a way that bears on the question asked.
predictionHint: Are people leaving the market typical of all residents on this issue?

stimulus: Orchard owner: My neighbor began releasing ladybugs among his apple trees to control aphids, and this year his harvest was larger than mine. Since my trees are the same kind as his and grow on similar land, I should expect that releasing ladybugs in my orchard would increase my harvest too.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether ladybugs are more expensive than the other methods of controlling aphids that are available
choices.B: Whether the neighbor sells his apples at a higher price per bushel than the owner does
choices.C: Whether the neighbor's ladybugs came from a commercial supplier or were collected locally
choices.D: Whether the neighbor's harvests already exceeded the owner's before he began releasing ladybugs
choices.E: Whether aphids are the only pest that damages apple trees in orchards of this region

explanations.A: Comparison shift: cost versus other methods is about whether ladybugs are a good buy, not about whether they raise a harvest.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the neighbor's selling price has no effect on whether ladybugs enlarge a harvest.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: where the ladybugs came from does not change whether they explain the larger harvest.
explanations.D: Correct. If the neighbor always harvested more, ladybugs probably do not explain this year's difference and the owner's expectation is weakened; if the harvests were similar before, the ladybugs gain credit.
explanations.E: Out of scope: whether other pests exist leaves untouched whether ladybugs made the difference.

keyTakeaway: In an argument from one case to another, ask whether the first case's advantage existed before the supposed cause was introduced.
predictionHint: Was the neighbor already ahead before the ladybugs?

stimulus: Researcher: At Halvorsen Corporation, employees who regularly use the on-site gym miss fewer days of work each year than employees who do not use it. This pattern shows that using the gym leads to fewer absences among the company's employees.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the gym is open during the lunch hour and on weekends as well as in the evening
choices.B: Whether absences at Halvorsen are lower than absences at other corporations of similar size
choices.C: Whether the number of days missed by each employee was recorded accurately
choices.D: Whether employees who use the gym are satisfied with its equipment
choices.E: Whether rarely absent employees were the ones likeliest to start using the gym

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: the gym's hours do not help decide whether gym use causes fewer absences.
explanations.B: Comparison shift: the argument compares gym users with non-users inside Halvorsen, not Halvorsen with other firms.
explanations.C: Premise booster: this questions the reliability of the data rather than the inference drawn from it.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: satisfaction with equipment says nothing about whether gym use reduces absences.
explanations.E: Correct. If rarely absent employees are the ones who start using the gym, the causation runs the other way and the conclusion is weakened; if not, the gym remains a plausible cause.

keyTakeaway: A correlation between two groups invites the reverse-direction question: did the outcome come first and shape who is in the group?
predictionHint: Do healthy, reliable people simply choose the gym?

stimulus: Transit agency report: Ridership on the Route 9 bus rose 18 percent in the year after the agency added a dedicated bus lane that shortened the typical trip by eight minutes. The shorter trips were therefore responsible for the rise in ridership.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the agency intends to build dedicated bus lanes on its other routes
choices.B: Whether ridership rose comparably during the same year on routes that got no new lane
choices.C: Whether Route 9 carried more riders than any other route before the lane was added
choices.D: Whether the time savings of eight minutes were measured during the morning rush hour on weekdays
choices.E: Whether the lane was paid for with city funds or with a federal grant

explanations.A: Out of scope: plans for other routes concern the future, while the conclusion concerns what caused a past increase.
explanations.B: Correct. If ridership rose similarly on routes without a lane, something citywide explains the increase and the shorter trips lose credit; if it did not, the lane is a likelier cause.
explanations.C: Comparison shift: Route 9's rank before the lane is a fixed comparison; the argument concerns a change over time.
explanations.D: Premise booster: this probes the measurement of the time savings, which the argument takes as given.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: the funding source has no bearing on why riders used the route more.

keyTakeaway: A before-and-after claim is best tested against a comparison group that did not receive the change.
predictionHint: Did similar routes without a lane also gain riders?

stimulus: Principal: Since Elm Grove Middle School introduced a mandatory homework-help hour each afternoon at the start of the school year, its students' average test scores have risen steadily. The homework-help hour has therefore improved the students' understanding of the material they are taught.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether most students enjoy the homework-help hour
choices.B: Whether students at nearby schools score higher on standardized tests than Elm Grove students do
choices.C: Whether teachers at the school are the ones who supervise the homework-help hour
choices.D: Whether the hour replaced a period that was previously used for physical education
choices.E: Whether the later tests were easier than the tests given before the hour began

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: enjoyment does not decide whether scores rose because understanding improved.
explanations.B: Comparison shift: how Elm Grove ranks against other schools is not the same as whether its own scores changed because of the hour.
explanations.C: Out of scope: who supervises the hour does not help decide whether it raised understanding.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: whether physical education was displaced, either way, leaves the link between the hour and the scores untouched.
explanations.E: Correct. If the later tests were easier, higher scores do not show better understanding and the conclusion is weakened; if the tests were comparable, the rise in scores better supports the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: When the evidence is a score and the conclusion is understanding, ask whether the measuring stick stayed the same.
predictionHint: Were the later tests of equal difficulty?

stimulus: City councilor: Downtown merchants are losing business because shoppers cannot find parking near the stores. A shuttle running between the city's large outlying lots and the downtown shopping district would solve this problem, so the city should fund such a shuttle.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether many shoppers who now avoid downtown over parking would use an outlying lot and a shuttle
choices.B: Whether downtown merchants would be willing to contribute part of the shuttle's operating costs if the city asked them to
choices.C: Whether other cities of comparable size operate shuttles in their downtown areas
choices.D: Whether parking fees downtown have risen in the last several years
choices.E: Whether the outlying lots together have more parking spaces than all of the downtown lots have

explanations.A: Correct. If shoppers would use park-and-ride, the shuttle solves the parking problem and the plan is supported; if they would refuse, the shuttle leaves the lost business where it was.
explanations.B: Out of scope: who shares the cost matters to financing, not to whether the shuttle solves the problem.
explanations.C: Out of scope: what other cities do says nothing about whether this shuttle would work here.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: a history of fee increases leaves unanswered whether shoppers would use a shuttle.
explanations.E: Comparison shift: the argument already calls the outlying lots large; their size relative to downtown lots is not the issue.

keyTakeaway: For a proposal, ask whether the people it is meant to help would actually take it up.
predictionHint: Would shoppers actually use a park-and-ride shuttle?

stimulus: Economist: Over the five years after adopting the Zendric accounting standard, the countries that adopted it saw foreign investment inflows rise by an average of 12 percent. Because the standard makes corporate finances more transparent, and foreign investors prefer transparent markets, adopting the standard must have caused the rise in inflows.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether foreign investors generally prefer markets in which corporate finances are transparent
choices.B: Whether implementing the standard is costly for the firms that must use it
choices.C: Whether the adopting countries' inflows were already rising at a similar rate before adoption
choices.D: Whether inflows rose more sharply in the fifth year after adoption than in the first
choices.E: Whether some of the adopting countries saw their inflows rise by more than 12 percent over those five years

explanations.A: Premise booster: the stimulus already states that investors prefer transparent markets, so this is information already given and no answer shifts the conclusion.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: the cost to firms does not bear on whether the standard raised foreign inflows.
explanations.C: Correct. If inflows were already rising at a similar rate, the standard may deserve no credit; if inflows had been flat or falling, the standard gains support as the cause of the rise.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: the timing of the rise within the five years does not help decide whether adoption caused it.
explanations.E: Extreme: an average of 12 percent is compatible with some countries exceeding it; learning that they did not change what explains the rise.

keyTakeaway: Discard any question whose answer the stimulus already supplies; the credited question targets the gap, usually a pre-existing trend.
predictionHint: Were inflows already trending upward before adoption?

stimulus: Hospital administrator: Before we introduced the preoperative checklist, 6 percent of our surgical patients developed infections. Since then, only 4 percent have. So the number of our patients who suffer surgical infections each year is now lower than it was before the checklist.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the infections that have occurred since the checklist have been less severe than those that occurred before it
choices.B: Whether the hospital's infection rate is now lower than the rates at comparable hospitals
choices.C: Whether the number of surgical patients treated each year has changed since the checklist was introduced
choices.D: Whether annual surgical volume is now at least one and a half times its level before the checklist
choices.E: Whether the proportion of surgical patients who develop infections fell by the same amount for every type of surgery

explanations.A: Shell game: severity is a neighbor of the measured quantity; the conclusion concerns the number of patients infected, not how bad each infection is.
explanations.B: Comparison shift: the argument compares the hospital with its own past, not with other hospitals.
explanations.C: Half right: a change in volume could go either way, so a Yes answer does not push the conclusion in one direction. The question must name a rise of a specific size.
explanations.D: Correct. At 1.5 times the volume, 4 percent equals the old 6 percent, so the number infected would not be lower; below that factor it would be. The answers swing the conclusion in opposite directions.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: the overall rates are given, and how the drop is spread across surgery types does not change the number infected.

keyTakeaway: When a percentage falls and the conclusion is about a count, the unstated base is the gap; find the size of change in the base that cancels the drop.
predictionHint: Rate fell from 6 to 4 percent; how much would the caseload have to grow to wipe out the gain?

stimulus: Dean: In last year's budget review, every one of the university's twelve academic departments reported lower per-student spending than in the year before. Because the university's overall per-student spending is just the combined result of what its departments spend on their students, it must have fallen last year as well.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the university's total enrollment grew over the course of the year
choices.B: Whether, over the year, enrollment moved substantially toward the departments with the highest per-student spending
choices.C: Whether the reductions in per-student spending were larger in some departments than in others
choices.D: Whether the largest departments are also the departments with the highest per-student spending
choices.E: Whether the reductions in spending were large enough to affect the quality of instruction

explanations.A: Out of scope: growth in total enrollment need not change the average spent per student, so neither answer moves the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. If students moved heavily toward the high-spending departments, the overall figure could rise even though each department's figure fell; if enrollment did not shift that way, the overall figure falls. The answers swing opposite ways.
explanations.C: Half right: unequal cuts do not matter if the mix of students stays put, because every department is still spending less per student.
explanations.D: Part versus whole: the static link between size and spending is tempting, but since every department cut spending, only a change in who enrolls where could offset the cuts.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: educational quality is a different topic from whether the overall per-student figure fell.

keyTakeaway: When every part falls but the conclusion is about the whole, ask whether the weighting of the parts changed.
predictionHint: Did students shift toward the departments that spend more?

stimulus: Retailer: In March we emailed a discount code to our 5,000 most frequent customers and sent nothing to our other 20,000 customers. By the end of April, 40 percent of the code recipients had made a purchase, compared with 25 percent of the other customers. The code therefore increased the likelihood that a customer would make a purchase.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the retailer's most frequent customers are more numerous than customers who buy only once a year
choices.B: Whether the retailer's records of which customers received the email were accurate
choices.C: Whether the 5,000 most frequent customers' usual two-month purchase rate was already close to 40 percent
choices.D: Whether the code recipients who made purchases spent more per purchase than the other customers who made purchases
choices.E: Whether the retailer plans to send discount codes to its other customers in the future

explanations.A: Out of scope: how many frequent customers exist compared with occasional ones does not bear on what caused the difference in purchase rates.
explanations.B: Premise booster: this questions the accuracy of the data the argument starts from instead of the inference drawn from it.
explanations.C: Correct. The recipients were chosen for being frequent buyers. If they already bought at close to 40 percent, the code did little and the conclusion is weakened; if their usual rate was far lower, the code likely raised it.
explanations.D: Shell game: the amount spent per purchase is a neighbor of the likelihood of purchasing and does not bear on whether more customers bought.
explanations.E: Out of scope: future mailings are irrelevant to what caused the results of this one.

keyTakeaway: When the treated group was picked rather than randomized, the best question asks what that group's baseline was before treatment.
predictionHint: Were the frequent customers already buying at about 40 percent?

stimulus: Councilmember: The city should not sell the old fire station to the developer who made the highest bid. The station has served the neighborhood for ninety years, and the residents, who use it for meetings and events, overwhelmingly want it kept as a community center.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: Public property should always be sold to whoever offers the highest price for it, whatever residents want.
choices.B: Publicly owned property that has long served a community should not be sold when the community overwhelmingly wants it kept.
choices.C: A city should never sell any building that it owns, whatever the circumstances or the wishes of residents.
choices.D: Cities should prefer buyers who plan to preserve historic buildings in their original condition.
choices.E: Decisions about the use of public property should be made by city officials rather than by the residents who are affected by them.

explanations.A: Opposite: this would require selling to the highest bidder, which is exactly what the councilmember rejects.
explanations.B: Correct. Every element has a referent in the case: publicly owned, long served the community, the community overwhelmingly wants it kept, and the verdict is not to sell.
explanations.C: Extreme: 'never sell any building' goes far beyond the one fire station, whose special features the councilmember emphasizes.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the argument never mentions historic preservation or original condition.
explanations.E: Reversal: the councilmember gives weight to what residents want, so a rule excluding them would undercut the reasoning.

keyTakeaway: A conforming principle fits every element of the case and reaches the case's verdict, and is no more extreme than the case supports.
predictionHint: Public property, long service, strong resident wish, so do not sell.

stimulus: Principle: A person who has promised to help someone with a task is obligated to follow through unless doing so would cause serious harm to a third party.
stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.A: Marisol promised a neighbor an airport ride. The drive will cost her an hour but harm no one, so she is obligated to give it.
choices.B: Dev promised to help a colleague move. Because helping would make him miss a dinner he had looked forward to all week, he is not obligated to help.
choices.C: Anita never promised to help her cousin study, but since helping would harm no one, she is obligated to help.
choices.D: Kofi promised to lend his car to a friend. Since the friend is unlicensed and would probably cause a serious accident, Kofi is obligated to lend it.
choices.E: Lena promised to help a neighbor paint a fence. She is not obligated to follow through because the neighbor never asked her to confirm.

explanations.A: Correct. She made a promise, the only cost is an inconvenience, and no third party is seriously harmed, so the exception does not apply and the rule's verdict of obligation holds.
explanations.B: Wrong force: missing a dinner is a minor cost to Dev, not serious harm to a third party, so the exception does not lift his obligation.
explanations.C: Reversal: Anita made no promise, so the trigger is absent and the rule issues no verdict about her.
explanations.D: Opposite: serious harm to a third party is exactly what lifts the obligation, so the rule does not say Kofi must lend the car.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the rule's only exception is serious harm to a third party; a missing confirmation does not release a promise.

keyTakeaway: To apply a rule, fill its trigger, check its exception, and then confirm that the choice gives the rule's own verdict.
predictionHint: Needed: a promise was made, no serious harm to a third party, so she must follow through.

stimulus: Principle: A journalist should refrain from publishing the name of a private individual who is suspected of a crime but has not been charged with it, unless publishing the name is necessary to avert an imminent threat to public safety.
stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.A: A journalist who published the name of a private individual charged with embezzlement was required to refrain, because publication could damage the individual's reputation.
choices.B: A journalist who withheld the name of an uncharged private individual suspected of a crime was wrong to do so, because the public wanted to know it.
choices.C: A journalist who published the name of an uncharged private individual suspected of repeated burglaries was not required to refrain, since further burglaries might occur.
choices.D: A journalist who published the name of an uncharged private individual suspected of planting a bomb that police had already defused was not required to refrain, since the bomb had endangered the public.
choices.E: A journalist who named an uncharged private individual suspected of poisoning food was not required to refrain, since only the name could warn residents before more tainted food reached stores.

explanations.A: Shell game: the individual here has been charged, so the rule's trigger is unmet and the rule does not say that the journalist was required to refrain.
explanations.B: Opposite: the rule tells journalists to refrain in this situation, and the public's wish to know is not the exception.
explanations.C: Half right: burglaries that merely might occur are not an imminent threat to public safety, and nothing says that publishing the name is necessary, so the exception is not filled.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the bomb has already been defused, so the threat is no longer imminent and publication is not necessary to avert it.
explanations.E: Correct. The individual is private, suspected and uncharged, so the trigger is met; but publishing is necessary to avert an imminent threat to public safety, so the exception fires and the duty to refrain is lifted.

keyTakeaway: An exception lifts the duty only when every word of its condition is met; look for 'necessary' and 'imminent' to be satisfied, not merely suggested.
predictionHint: Look for the case where the trigger is met and the exception's necessity and imminence are both stated.

stimulus: Ombudsman: The pension board acted improperly in denying Mr. Quill's claim. The board relied on an eligibility rule that it adopted only after Quill had retired, and Quill had retired in reliance on the eligibility rules then in force.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: A board acts improperly if it denies a benefit under a rule that was adopted after the claim was filed.
choices.B: A board that adopts a new eligibility rule is obliged to give prior notice to everyone whom the rule could affect.
choices.C: A board acts improperly only if it denies a benefit under a rule adopted after the claimant acted in reliance on the rules then in force.
choices.D: A board acts improperly if it denies a benefit under a rule adopted after the claimant acted in reliance on the rules then in force.
choices.E: A board acts improperly if it denies a benefit to a claimant who has made a substantial contribution toward it.

explanations.A: Shell game: the stimulus says the rule was adopted after Quill retired, not after his claim was filed; nothing places the claim's filing date relative to the rule, so the case does not fill this principle.
explanations.B: Wrong part: giving notice of a new rule is a different duty from the one broken here, and the ombudsman does not mention notice.
explanations.C: Necessary versus sufficient: 'only if' gives a requirement for impropriety, so it cannot establish that the denial was improper even when the case meets that requirement.
explanations.D: Correct. Every element has a referent: denial of a benefit, a rule adopted later, reliance by the claimant, and the verdict of impropriety. As a sufficient condition, it lets the conclusion follow.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the stimulus says nothing about Quill's contributions, so no element of this principle appears in the case.

keyTakeaway: A principle that justifies a conclusion must be sufficient: if its conditions hold in the case, the verdict follows; 'only if' phrasing fails.
predictionHint: If a rule is adopted after someone relied on the earlier rules, denying a benefit under it is improper.

stimulus:
Curator: The museum should accept the Brennan estate's donation of landscape paintings. Each painting is of genuine artistic merit, and a museum has a duty to preserve works of merit whenever it is able to do so.

Registrar: I agree that we should accept them, but not for that reason. A museum has no general duty to preserve works of merit, even when it has room to keep them. We should accept these paintings because we happen to have the storage space and because they will draw the visitors we badly need.
stem: The curator and the registrar disagree over whether

choices.A: the museum should accept the Brennan estate's donation of landscape paintings
choices.B: the paintings in the donation are in fact of genuine artistic merit, as the curator says
choices.C: a museum has a duty to preserve works of merit whenever it can
choices.D: the paintings will draw visitors whom the museum badly needs to attract this year
choices.E: the museum has enough storage space to keep all of the paintings in the donation

explanations.A: Both speakers say the donation should be accepted. The registrar opens with 'I agree,' so this is a point of agreement, not disagreement.
explanations.B: Question mark: the curator affirms it, but the registrar never disputes the merit of the paintings.
explanations.C: Correct. The curator affirms that being able to preserve works of merit creates a duty; the registrar denies that any such general duty exists, even when the museum has room. One Yes and one No.
explanations.D: Question mark: the registrar affirms it, but the curator says nothing about visitors.
explanations.E: Question mark: the registrar affirms it, but the curator never mentions storage space.

keyTakeaway: When speakers agree on the conclusion, the dispute lives in the reasoning; check which principle one affirms and the other denies.
predictionHint: They agree to accept the paintings but disagree about the duty the curator uses as a reason.

stimulus: Planner: The city of Orsk replaced its downtown parking minimums with a flat permit fee, and over the next three years the number of new cafes and shops downtown rose steadily. Talvane's downtown resembles Orsk's in size, in the age of its buildings, and in the number of vacant storefronts. Talvane should therefore adopt a flat permit fee, since doing so will likewise bring new businesses downtown.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the planner's argument?

choices.A: Orsk's population is about twice that of Talvane.
choices.B: Some Orsk shop owners objected to the flat permit fee when it was first proposed.
choices.C: Orsk's strictly enforced parking minimums had been widely blamed for deterring new businesses, while Talvane's are routinely waived.
choices.D: Several other cities that replaced their parking minimums with flat fees also saw the number of new downtown businesses increase in the years that followed.
choices.E: The flat fee that Talvane would charge would be collected by a different city department than the one that collects it in Orsk.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: a difference in total population says nothing about whether the fee was what drew businesses, so the shared features the planner cites still stand.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: early objections from some owners do not bear on whether openings followed from the fee itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The fee worked in Orsk, on this account, by lifting a binding burden. If Talvane's minimums are routinely waived, there is no comparable burden to lift, so the feature that produced the result in Orsk is missing in Talvane.
explanations.D: Opposite: this adds further cases in which the same step was followed by openings, which strengthens the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope: which department collects the fee does not touch what makes the fee attract businesses.

keyTakeaway: An analogy is broken by a difference that touches the mechanism, not by any difference at all.
predictionHint: Ask what the policy did in Orsk to produce the result, then look for a reason Talvane lacks that.

stimulus: Critic: Some defend novelists who draw on the private lives of real acquaintances without permission, saying that the details are merely raw material for fiction. But by that reasoning a portrait painter could put a stranger's face on a billboard without consent, since a face is merely raw material for art. Surely no one would say that the painter does nothing wrong.
stem: The critic's argument proceeds by

choices.A: showing that a justification offered for one practice would equally justify a clearly objectionable parallel practice
choices.B: pointing out that the defenders' position conflicts with a law governing the profession of novelist
choices.C: arguing that novelists deserve less protection than painters because their work reaches more people
choices.D: inferring that a practice is wrong from the fact that most people who have considered it disapprove of it
choices.E: generalizing from the single case of a portrait painter to the claim that every use of a real person's likeness in any art form is wrong

explanations.A: Correct. The critic takes the defenders' own rationale (the details are merely raw material) and applies it to a parallel case, the billboard, where the conclusion is plainly unacceptable, thereby discrediting the rationale.
explanations.B: Out of scope: no law or professional rule is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
explanations.C: Comparison shift: the critic never ranks novelists against painters or mentions how far their work travels; the painter is used as a parallel, not as a contrast.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the critic cites no poll or majority opinion; the appeal is to a single case that 'no one would say' is acceptable.
explanations.E: Half right: the painter case is used, but only to test the defenders' rationale. The critic does not conclude that every use of a likeness in art is wrong, which is far broader than anything claimed.

keyTakeaway: When an arguer says 'by that reasoning,' the method is a parallel built to show the original reasoning proves too much.
predictionHint: The defenders' reason is turned onto a different case where everyone rejects the result.

stimulus: Pharmacologist: In experiments, a compound that suppresses the protein Kell-4 prevented the muscle wasting that normally follows prolonged bed rest in mice. The compound is known to suppress Kell-4 in human cells as well as in mouse cells, and prolonged bed rest also causes muscle wasting in humans. So the compound will probably prevent muscle wasting in bedridden humans.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the pharmacologist's argument?

choices.A: Most of the genes found in mice have close counterparts in humans.
choices.B: The compound caused no harmful side effects in the mice that received it.
choices.C: Kell-4 is present in human muscle tissue at concentrations roughly similar to those found in mouse muscle tissue, and it is made by similar cells.
choices.D: In humans as in mice, the muscle wasting that follows prolonged bed rest is brought about chiefly by increased Kell-4 activity.
choices.E: Several compounds that prevent muscle wasting in mice have failed to do so in humans.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: overall genetic similarity does not show that the specific process behind wasting is shared.
explanations.B: Out of scope: safety in the mice has no bearing on whether the compound works against wasting in humans.
explanations.C: Half right: Kell-4 being present at similar levels shows the protein exists in humans, not that it plays the role in wasting that it plays in mice.
explanations.D: Correct. The result in mice depended on Kell-4 driving the wasting. This says the same driver operates in humans, and the compound is already stated to suppress it there, so the shared mechanism is secured.
explanations.E: Opposite: past failures to carry results from mice to humans make the analogy less trustworthy.

keyTakeaway: Strengthen an analogy by confirming the shared mechanism, not by adding more similarities.
predictionHint: The argument needs Kell-4 to be what causes wasting in humans too.

stimulus: Consultant: After the Brightwell hospital group merged its three billing offices into one, its collection rate rose sharply. The Marlow school district likewise runs three separate transportation offices, so merging them into one will raise the district's on-time bus rate.
stem: The consultant's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: The merged Brightwell billing office handled more accounts than any one of the three former offices had handled before the merger took place.
choices.B: The way in which merging the offices raised Brightwell's collection rate does not depend on a feature specific to billing work.
choices.C: No transportation office in the district has ever raised the district's on-time bus rate on its own.
choices.D: Brightwell's collection rate had been below the average for hospital groups before the merger.
choices.E: Merging offices is the only step that would raise the district's on-time bus rate.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the number of accounts handled bears on Brightwell's size, not on whether the merger's effect would carry over to buses.
explanations.B: Correct. If the improvement came from something peculiar to billing, the Marlow merger would not reproduce it. Denying this choice breaks the analogy, so the argument requires it.
explanations.C: Extreme: the argument does not need a history of failure in the district; it needs only that the merger would help.
explanations.D: Out of scope: Brightwell's rank before the merger does not bear on whether the same mechanism applies to school buses.
explanations.E: Necessary versus sufficient: the argument says merging will raise the rate, not that merging is the only way to do so.

keyTakeaway: An analogy's necessary assumption is that the mechanism behind the result is not specific to the original case.
predictionHint: The consultant needs Marlow's offices to be susceptible to whatever helped Brightwell.

stimulus: Tourism board: The average amount each visitor to Kellmar Island spent during a stay was fifteen percent higher this year than last year. Tourism revenue on the island therefore rose this year.
stem: The tourism board's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: The number of visits to the island did not fall at all.
choices.B: Every visitor spent more this year than the same visitor spent last year.
choices.C: Visitors to Kellmar spent more per stay than visitors to neighboring islands did.
choices.D: The rise in spending was caused chiefly by higher prices on the island rather than by visitors buying more goods and services.
choices.E: The number of visits to the island did not fall by enough to cancel the rise in spending per visit.

explanations.A: Necessary versus sufficient: no decline would guarantee the conclusion, but a small decline is compatible with it, so 'at all' demands too much.
explanations.B: Wrong part: the premise concerns an average, so some visitors may have spent less. The conclusion does not need every visitor to spend more.
explanations.C: Comparison shift: the argument compares this year with last year on one island, not Kellmar with other islands.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the reason for the higher spending does not affect whether total revenue rose.
explanations.E: Correct. Revenue depends on spending per visit and the number of visits. A rise in the first yields a rise in revenue only if the second did not drop enough to wipe it out; if visits did fall that much, the conclusion fails.

keyTakeaway: A change in an average or rate supports a change in a total only if the other factor in the product did not move enough to offset it.
predictionHint: Revenue is visits times spending; the board has told us only about spending.

stimulus: Mayor: Admission to the city's parks is free, since no one is ever charged an entry fee. It follows that running the parks costs the city nothing.
stem: The mayor's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on the unsupported claim of a single official rather than on the city's public financial records or any independent audit
choices.B: moves from the parks being free of charge to visitors to the parks being costless to the city
choices.C: treats the absence of an entry fee as proof that the parks are popular
choices.D: fails to consider that entry fees may be charged for special events, concerts, or guided tours held inside the parks
choices.E: assumes that the parks benefit every resident of the city equally

explanations.A: Out of scope: the problem lies in the logic from premise to conclusion, not in who states the premise.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Free' in the premise means that visitors pay nothing; the conclusion needs the parks to cost the city nothing. The same word covers two different ideas, and the argument slides from one to the other.
explanations.C: Shell game: popularity is not mentioned in the argument and plays no role in it.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: even if special-event fees exist, the leap from no entry fee to no cost to the city remains.
explanations.E: Out of scope: how widely the parks benefit residents has nothing to do with who pays for them.

keyTakeaway: When a word like 'free' appears in the premise and the conclusion, check that it means the same thing both times.
predictionHint: Free for whom?

stimulus: Most residents of Brandt believe that the town's tap water is free of contaminants. Therefore, the tap water in Brandt is free of contaminants.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: assumes that Brandt's residents are an unusually well-informed group
choices.B: confuses the water's being safe to drink with its being free of contaminants
choices.C: takes the fact that many people believe something as establishing that it is true
choices.D: overlooks that a minority of residents may hold a different belief about the water
choices.E: presumes that contaminants are the only threat to the quality of tap water

explanations.A: Out of scope: the flaw is present however well informed the residents are; belief is not the same as fact.
explanations.B: Shell game: the argument never uses 'safe to drink' at all, so no confusion between the two is in play.
explanations.C: Correct. The premise reports what residents believe; the conclusion states how the water actually is. What people believe can be false.
explanations.D: Wrong force: even if every resident held the belief, the same gap between belief and fact would remain.
explanations.E: Out of scope: other threats to water quality are not part of this argument.

keyTakeaway: A claim about what people believe cannot, by itself, establish what is true.
predictionHint: Belief in the premise, fact in the conclusion.

stimulus: Every member of the zoning board knows that the proposed tower would block the view from Harbor Park. Some members of the board hope the tower will be approved. Priya is a member of the zoning board.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Priya hopes that the tower will be approved.
choices.B: Priya wants to prevent the tower from being built.
choices.C: Every member of the zoning board opposes the tower.
choices.D: Priya has toured Harbor Park to see the view for herself.
choices.E: The proposed tower would block the view from Harbor Park.

explanations.A: Out of scope: only some members hope for approval, and Priya is not said to be one of them.
explanations.B: Out of scope: knowing that the view would be blocked says nothing about whether she wants the tower stopped.
explanations.C: Extreme: some members hope for approval, so not every member can oppose the tower.
explanations.D: Out of scope: nothing says how Priya came to know what she knows.
explanations.E: Correct. 'Knows' is factive: no one can know something false. Since every member, Priya included, knows the tower would block the view, it would.

keyTakeaway: 'Knows' and 'realizes' carry the truth of what follows them; 'believes' and 'hopes' do not.
predictionHint: Which verb in the stimulus guarantees its content?

stimulus: Councilor: The city's safety program was designed to reduce workplace injuries at the Corvane plant. Therefore, the plant now has fewer workplace injuries than it did before the program began.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the councilor's argument?

choices.A: The number of workplace injuries at the plant is higher this year than it was before the program began.
choices.B: The safety program cost the city considerably less than it was originally projected to cost when the council approved it.
choices.C: Most workers at the plant say that they support the safety program.
choices.D: Other cities have adopted safety programs similar to the one in Corvane.
choices.E: The designers of the program had previously worked on safety programs at other plants.

explanations.A: Correct. The argument moves from what the program was meant to do to what happened. Evidence that injuries are in fact higher shows the intention was not realized.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the program's cost says nothing about whether injuries fell.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: worker support is not the same as results.
explanations.D: Out of scope: what other cities did has no bearing on this plant's injuries.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the designers' background might support the program, but does not weaken the claim.

keyTakeaway: Designed to, meant to, and intended to describe a goal, not an outcome.
predictionHint: The councilor treats an aim as a result; show that the result did not follow.

stimulus: Driving instructor: In a survey of drivers who have completed the Meridian defensive-driving course, a large majority said they feel more confident behind the wheel than they did before the course. This shows that the course makes its graduates safer drivers.
stem: The instructor's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Graduates of the course drive more often than drivers who have not taken it.
choices.B: Confidence behind the wheel is the most reliable single predictor of how safely a person will drive over the long term.
choices.C: Every graduate of the course feels more confident behind the wheel than before the course.
choices.D: Graduates' increased confidence is not, in the main, merely a matter of overestimating their driving ability.
choices.E: Before taking the course, its graduates were less safe drivers than other drivers were.

explanations.A: Out of scope: how often graduates drive does not link their confidence to their safety.
explanations.B: Extreme: the argument needs confidence to track safety here, not to be the single best predictor of it.
explanations.C: Wrong part: the survey found a 'large majority', and the conclusion does not need every graduate to be more confident.
explanations.D: Correct. The survey reports a feeling; the conclusion concerns actual safety. If the gain in confidence were chiefly an overestimate of skill, the survey would give no reason to think graduates drive more safely.
explanations.E: Out of scope: graduates' earlier driving relative to others is irrelevant to whether the course improved them.

keyTakeaway: When the evidence is how people feel and the conclusion is how things are, the missing link is that the feeling is accurate.
predictionHint: Confidence must reflect real improvement rather than overestimation.

stimulus: Each part in the Callis X-9 engine has been rated the most durable part of its kind on the market. Therefore, the Callis X-9 is the most durable engine on the market.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on ratings that were all supplied by a single source
choices.B: assumes that a whole must have a property merely because each of its parts has that property
choices.C: confuses the durability of an engine with its performance
choices.D: overlooks that some of the engine's parts may be rated lower than competing parts on features other than durability
choices.E: presumes that durability is the only feature buyers care about in an engine

explanations.A: Out of scope: the number of rating sources is not mentioned and is not the gap.
explanations.B: Correct. Every part being the most durable of its kind does not guarantee that the engine they form is the most durable engine, since how the parts are combined also matters.
explanations.C: Shell game: the argument never speaks of performance.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: ratings on other features do not touch a conclusion about durability.
explanations.E: Out of scope: buyers' preferences are not part of the argument.

keyTakeaway: What holds of every part need not hold of the whole they form.
predictionHint: Parts excellent, therefore whole excellent: composition.

stimulus: The Vance Quartet is among the finest chamber ensembles in the country. So its cellist, Ira Dahl, must be among the finest cellists in the country.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Ira Dahl has performed with other ensembles besides the Vance Quartet.
choices.B: The cello is more difficult to play than the other instruments in a quartet.
choices.C: Most of the finest chamber ensembles in the country have exactly four members.
choices.D: The Vance Quartet performs more often than other chamber ensembles in the country.
choices.E: A chamber ensemble cannot be among the finest in the country unless each of its members is among the finest players of the instrument he or she plays.

explanations.A: Out of scope: Dahl's other engagements do not connect the ensemble's quality to his own.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the relative difficulty of instruments is not at issue.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the number of members in other ensembles does not bear on Dahl's standing.
explanations.D: Out of scope: how often the quartet performs does not link the group's ranking to its cellist's ranking.
explanations.E: Correct. The argument passes from a quality of the whole to a quality of one part. It works only if a group of that standing needs every member to be of that standing.

keyTakeaway: A conclusion about a part drawn from a fact about the whole needs a premise that the whole's quality passes down to each member.
predictionHint: Whole to part: what bridges them?

stimulus: Each player on Orion FC earns more than the average player in the league. Therefore, Orion's total player payroll is larger than that of the typical club in the league.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Orion's players are, on average, older than the players on most other clubs.
choices.B: The average salary paid to players in the league has risen sharply in recent years.
choices.C: Orion has far fewer players on its roster than the typical club in the league has.
choices.D: Orion's players receive large bonuses in addition to their salaries.
choices.E: Orion's ticket revenue is lower than that of most clubs in the league.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the age of the players does not affect how large the total payroll is.
explanations.B: Out of scope: a league-wide rise in salaries does not distinguish Orion from other clubs.
explanations.C: Correct. A total depends on how many players there are as well as how much each earns. A small roster could keep the total below the typical club's even if every player is well paid.
explanations.D: Opposite: bonuses would raise Orion's payroll, which supports the conclusion.
explanations.E: Out of scope: revenue from tickets is not part of the player payroll.

keyTakeaway: A total depends on the number of parts as well as on the size of each.
predictionHint: The conclusion is about a sum; the premise is about each member.

stimulus: Critic: The Eastgate Museum's collection is worth more, in total, than the collection of any other museum in the country. Hence the typical work in Eastgate's collection is worth more than the typical work in any other museum's collection.
stem: The critic's reasoning is flawed in that it

choices.A: treats a collection's total value as indicating the value of its typical work, though the total depends partly on the number of works
choices.B: assumes that monetary worth is the only legitimate measure of the value of a work of art, ignoring aesthetic and historical significance
choices.C: relies on the opinion of a critic rather than on that of professional appraisers
choices.D: fails to establish that Eastgate's works are better known than the works of other museums
choices.E: concludes that every work in the collection is valuable from the fact that some of its works are

explanations.A: Correct. A collection can be worth the most in total simply by being large. The premise concerns the whole's total; the conclusion concerns the typical part.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the argument and its premise already use monetary worth; whether it is the only measure is not the gap.
explanations.C: Out of scope: who supplied the claim is not the problem; the inference fails regardless of the source.
explanations.D: Shell game: how well known the works are is never mentioned.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the conclusion is about the typical work, not about every work, and the premise is not about some works.

keyTakeaway: A property of a total does not transfer to each member when the number of members could explain it.
predictionHint: Total value versus value per work.

stimulus: County analyst: Our recycling program inspected the bins of 300 households. The households volunteered in response to a county mailing, and volunteers were recruited from each district in proportion to its population. Using a single written standard, inspectors judged that 85 percent of the volunteers' bins were sorted carefully. We can conclude that most households in the county sort their recycling carefully.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the analyst's argument?

choices.A: Whether the county's recycling program has more participants now than it had in previous years
choices.B: Whether 300 households is enough to permit an estimate of the county-wide rate that is accurate to within a few percentage points
choices.C: Whether the districts from which the volunteers came differ in the amount of recycling they generate
choices.D: Whether households that sort their recycling carefully were more likely than other households to volunteer for inspection
choices.E: Whether the households whose bins were judged careless were later told the results of the inspection

explanations.A: Out of scope: the number of participants over time says nothing about whether volunteers resemble nonvolunteers.
explanations.B: Half right: sample size can matter, but a sample of 300 is not the weak point here; a sample that is large and self-selected remains unrepresentative.
explanations.C: Out of scope: volume of recycling per district does not bear on how carefully households sort, and the volunteers were already spread by population.
explanations.D: Correct. The volunteers chose to be inspected. If careful sorters were more inclined to volunteer, the 85 percent figure overstates the county rate; if volunteering was unrelated to sorting habits, it supports the conclusion.
explanations.E: Out of scope: whether households were informed afterward does not affect the inspection results.

keyTakeaway: When people choose to be in the sample, ask whether choosing is related to the trait being measured.
predictionHint: Volunteers: do they differ from non-volunteers in sorting?

stimulus: Port authority: Dredging the Calloway channel would let larger cargo ships dock, raising the port's annual revenue by an estimated eight percent. A gain of that size makes dredging clearly worthwhile for the region.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the port authority's argument?

choices.A: Dredging the channel would cost the port authority several million dollars in construction expenses and in later maintenance work.
choices.B: Dredging projects at other ports have raised those ports' revenue by more than eight percent.
choices.C: Several environmental groups have criticized the dredging proposal.
choices.D: The channel was last dredged more than thirty years ago.
choices.E: Dredging would destroy the oyster beds that sustain a regional fishing industry whose yearly earnings exceed the port's projected gain.

explanations.A: Half right: a cost is another entry in the ledger, but no figure shows it exceeds the gain, so it does not establish that the project is not worthwhile.
explanations.B: Opposite: larger gains elsewhere make the projected gain more believable.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: criticism by groups does not show what dredging would cost the region.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the date of the last dredging has no bearing on whether the benefits outweigh the harms.
explanations.E: Correct. The conclusion rests on one benefit. This puts a large harm on the other side of the scale, one stated to be bigger than the benefit, so the project may not be worthwhile for the region.

keyTakeaway: A worth-it conclusion is weakened by a cost shown to be comparable to or larger than the benefit; a bare cost is not enough.
predictionHint: Look for a harm that is at least as big as the revenue gain, and that falls on the region.

stimulus: City official: The composting program was introduced solely to cut the city's greenhouse-gas emissions. Yet collecting food scraps requires trucks to make additional trips, and those trips add emissions. The program has therefore failed in its purpose and should be scrapped.
stem: The official's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: treats an emissions cost of the program as decisive without weighing it against the emissions the program avoids
choices.B: relies on the claim that greenhouse-gas emissions are harmful without establishing that they actually damage the environment
choices.C: infers that a program has failed from the fact that it has not yet met every one of its goals
choices.D: ignores the financial cost of operating the composting program
choices.E: draws a conclusion about the whole city from the experience of only a few of the neighborhoods the program serves

explanations.A: Correct. The program's purpose is a net reduction. The official counts only the emissions it adds, with no look at the emissions it may prevent, so the claim that it has failed is unsupported.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the argument takes the goal as given; whether the goal is worthwhile is not at issue.
explanations.C: Shell game: the program has one stated goal, not several, so the argument is not about unmet goals.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the argument judges the program by its stated purpose, emissions, so financial cost does not bear on it.
explanations.E: Out of scope: nothing in the passage restricts the evidence to a few neighborhoods.

keyTakeaway: Counting one cost is not weighing; ask what sits on the other side of the ledger.
predictionHint: Added emissions, but what about emissions avoided?

stimulus: Consultant: Switching Wexley Clinic from paper records to an electronic system would free about 2,000 staff-hours of filing work each year. The clinic should therefore make the switch.
stem: The consultant's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: No other change the clinic could make, whether to records or to scheduling, would free as many staff-hours each year as the electronic system would.
choices.B: The staff-hours that the electronic system freed would be spent on patient care.
choices.C: The cost of adopting and running the electronic system is not greater than the worth of the staff time it would free.
choices.D: Most clinics that have switched to electronic records have saved staff time.
choices.E: Staff time is the most valuable resource that a clinic has.

explanations.A: Comparison shift: the conclusion is that the switch is worth making, not that it is the best of all possible changes, so no ranking is required.
explanations.B: Half right: how the hours are used might matter, but if they were put to other worthwhile uses the conclusion would still hold.
explanations.C: Correct. The consultant lists only a benefit. For 'should' to follow, the cost of the switch must not swamp that benefit; if it did, the clinic would be better off staying on paper.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: other clinics' experience is not required for the claim about this clinic.
explanations.E: Extreme: the argument needs the freed time to be worth something against the cost, not to be a clinic's single most valuable resource.

keyTakeaway: A recommendation that cites only a benefit needs the assumption that the costs do not outweigh it.
predictionHint: The costs of switching are missing from the consultant's ledger.
